Please see our response to your question.
Questions:
Q1: Does this apply to students whose DLl is not specifically mentioned on a study permit? For example, DLI Alberta?
A1: Yes, the regulation applies to all study permit holders regardless of whether their DLl is specifically mentioned on their study permit or not.
Q2: If a student is withdrawn from the program, and their study permit becomes invalid, can they/do they need to apply to restore their status as a student if they are accepted into another program at the same DLl shortly after the withdrawal?
A2: A study permit holder must meet their study permit conditions. In such cases where the student is withdrawn due to not meeting previous study permit conditions, the student is considered "no longer enrolled". If you do not abide to the conditions of your study permit you may need to change your status, or leave Canada. However, there are a few cases where a student may be able to take a leave of up to a maximum of 150 days from their program of studies and still be actively pursuing their studies.
For more information, please refer to the [RCC website.
Q3: Sometimes students could be withdrawn for non-payment, but after paying the fees in full, they could be reinstated. It could take about a week for us to re-instate the student. In this case, does their study permit become invalid the day they are withdrawn, or they can continue studying after being reinstated?
A3: See above.
Q4: What is IRCC's definition of enrolment for the purpose of this provision? Is it being active in the program or being enrolled in and taking classes? Students could be active in the program while on a scheduled break or an authorized leave, but they are not enrolled in classes during that time.
A4: A student is considered enrolled if they are actively attending classes or registered for courses at their DLl excluding regularly scheduled breaks, and authorized leave of up to 150 days. Students will need to ensure that they meet the conditions of their study permit Your conditions as a study permit holder in Canada-Canada.ca. Therefore, while students are not actively taking classes during regularly scheduled breaks or authorized leave of up to 150 days, they are still considered as being enrolled in their DLI.
Sincerely,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

De : Envoyé : 28 janvier 2025 15:22 À : Objet : RE: Online courses and PGWP-REP-2024-1340- Due 3-Sep-24
Hello!
The recently announced IRCC regulations indicate that international students with valid study permits may need to apply for a new study permit when changing their designated learning institution (DLl) in most situations. However, there are scenarios (below) that do not clearly align with the examples provided on the IRCC guidelines page. [https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/study-canada/change-schools.html](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/study-canada/change-schools.html)
1. Scenario 1: Prerequisite Courses at a Secondary Institution A student is currently enrolled in a degree program at a university (DLI) but requires prerequisite high school courses. These courses would be attended simultaneously at a secondary school while the student remains enrolled in their degree program at the university. Since the student is not changing their primary institution but is attending a single course at a secondary school, would they still be required to apply for a new study permit to take this course?
A: Secondary students whose permit only authorizes studies at the primary or secondary level must apply for a new study permit in order to pursue studies at the post-secondary level. This also applies to post-secondary study permit holders, whose permit names a DLl or limits their studies to the post-secondary level, who wish to attend a secondary school program/course, even though the student is not changing their primary institution. Therefore, individuals transitioning between post-secondary and secondary level need to get a new study permit by applying to extend their current one to attend a secondary school.
and Cizenship Caneda
2.Scenario 2: Cross-Institutional Enrollment for a Single Course Some students encounter situations where a required course is unavailable at their current university (DLl). In such cases, they obtain a letter of permission from their primary institution to take the course at another DLI (university) for one term, with the intention of transferring the credit back to their primary DLI (the one listed on their study permit). In this scenario, since the student is not permanently changing their DLl but is only attending a single course at another institution temporarily,would they need to apply for a new study permit?
A: Since November 08, 2024, post-secondary study permit holders must be enrolled at the designated learning institution (DLl) named on their permit. If a study permit holder wishes to concurrently attend more than one DLl, they must apply for a study permit for each DLl at which they intend to study.
As these scenarios are not explicitly addressed in the current guidelines, clarification on these matters would greatly help us provide accurate advice to international students.
Thank you for your guidance.
Regards,

threads.answer:
ATTENTION: This e-mail originated from outside of
Good day,
Thank you for contacting the Immigration Representatives Mailbox.
Please note that this mailbox is intended for general guidance and does not provide responses to case-specific inquiries but have provided the following information as guidance. If you have case specific questions about a file, you are encouraged to submit the IRCC Web form
Please see our response to your question.
Follow up question: Do I understand this correctly that if a student's study permit becomes invalid due to being withdrawn from their DLl, they lose their valid status in Canada? If yes, they are not authorized to change their status with Canada. If this is the case, do they need to:
In case they want to restore their status as a student, apply for a study permit restoration? In case they want to change their status to a visitor, apply for a restoration and a visitor's record?
Answer: A student is no longer registered or enrolled when the DLl has sent a letter informing the student that they've been dismissed, withdrawn or transferred to another institution. Their study permit becomes invalid as per R222(1)(a.1), even if the document is not expired. Therefore, they would need to change their status or leave Canada. Please note that applying for a restoration would only be possible if the document has expired. A foreign national has 90 days from the date of expiry date to submit a restoration application.
Q4: What is IRCC's definition of enrolment for the purpose of this provision? Is it being active in the program or being enrolled in and taking classes? Students could be active in the program while on a scheduled break or an authorized leave, but they are not enrolled in classes during that time. A4: A student is considered enrolled if they are actively attending classes or registered
for courses at their DLl excluding regularly scheduled breaks, and authorized leave of up
to 150 days. Students will need to ensure that they meet the conditions of their study
permit Your conditions as a study permit holder in Canada-Canada.ca. Therefore, while
students are not actively taking classes during regularly scheduled breaks or authorized
leave of up to 150 days, they are still considered as being enrolled in their DLI. Follow up questions:
If a student is registered in classes, but starts their program in let's say four months, are they considered enrolled at a DLI by IRCC for the purpose of this regulation for four months
until they start classes? Every term, we have several students who are withdrawn from a
program, but are planning to start a different program in one term.
If a student is withdrawn from a program, has a LOA for a different program that starts in 4 months, but is not registered in classes yet, are they considered enrolled at a DLl by IRCC
for the purpose of this regulation for four months until they start classes?
Answer: As indicated above, a student is no longer registered or enrolled when the DLl has sent a letter informing the student that they've been dismissed, withdrawn or transferred to another institution. Their study permit becomes invalid as per R222(1)(a.1), even if the document is not expired. Please note that an academic withdrawal is not considered an authorized leave in which the student is no longer considered an active student. Therefore, they would need to change their status or leave Canada.
In comparison, an academic suspension would be considered a leave. A student may take leave for a maximum 150 days due to academic suspension and would not be considered as no longer being registered or enrolled. The student would be allowed to return to their studies after the suspension. Please note that the enrollment status as " no longer registered/enrolled" and " academic suspension" are not the same. Please note that any leave over 150 days is not allowed, and the student would either need to change their status or leave Canada.
The IRCC website provides a glossary with definitions about the enrollment status of a student at a DLl such as academic suspension, no longer registered or enrolled, authorized leave etc.
Thank you kindly,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.answer:
Good day,
Thank you for contacting the Immigration Represe ntatives Mailbox.
Please note that this mailbox is intended for general guidance and does not provide responses to case-specific inquiries but have provided the following information as guidance. Ifyou have case specific questions about a file, you are encouraged to submit the IRCC Web form.
Please see our response to your question.
*** Section 2 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR) defines a marriage as follows:
marriage, in respect of a marriage that took place outside Canada, means a marriage that is valid both under the laws of the jurisdiction where it took place and under Canadian law.
The spousal guide indicates that that a marriage must be legally recognized in the country where it is performed and applicants are asked to provide a copy of their marriage certificate demonstrating that the marriage was legally registered with the government where it took place. The onus is on the applicant to provide sufficient proof of their marriage when applying as a spouse under the family class.
For more information regarding the legality of marriages, see : Processing spouses and common-law partners: Assessing the legality of a marriage-Canada.ca
In terms of what to do if a marriage is not legally recognized where it occurred or in cases where clients are unable to legally register their marriage, applicants can consider the following options:
- * re-marry in another jurisdiction where their marriage would be legal
* apply and/or be processed under either the common-law partner or conjugal partner category of the family class if the relationship between the applicant and sponsor is genuine and meets the legal requirements of either of these categories. The applicant must meet the definition of common-law partner or conjugal partner at the time the sponsorship and permanent residence applications are submitted, (i.e. for common-law partners, they must have lived together continuously in a conjugal relationship for at least one year, and for conjugal partners, they must have been in a conjugal relationship for at least one year).
It should be noted that if the application has already been submitted under the spouse category of the family class, an officer is not required to automatically re-assess an application based on different family class marital/conjugal relationship between the applicant and the sponsor than the one identified on the original application. The onus is on the applicant to inform the department of any circumstances or considerations relevant to their case. The processing officer will consider this on a case-by-case basis. An officer must continue to be satisfied that the relationship meets legal requirements and is genuine.
If the applicant is unwilling to be considered as a common-law or conjugal partner, or is unable to provide satisfactory evidence of a common-law or conjugal relationship, the application may be refused.
Alternatively, people who would not normally be eligible to become permanent residents of Canada may have the option to request consideration on humanitarian and compassionate grounds. Requesting H&C consideration is an exceptional measure – it is not simply another means of applying for permanent resident status. The H&C decision-making process is highly discretionary and H&C requests are assessed by officers on a case-by-case basis. There is no guarantee of approval. For more information see: Humanitarian and compassionate consideration and Humanitarian and compassionate: processing applications from outside Canada.
We hope you find this information useful.
Thank you kindly,

Based on this definition:
a. Would there be any difference if the applicant was travelling from a country other than the US or St. Pierre and Miquelon?

Would this be accurate?

. A CBSA officer advised that an individual would not be deemed as a flagpoler if legally admitted to the USA (vs. administrative refusal). Would this be accurate?

threads.answer:
Yes, there is a difference, these applicants would not be flagpoling.
2. Would the time duration spent outside of Canada make any difference? E.g., instead of travelling and submitting an application at the border the same day, the applicant was in the US for several weeks.

The amount of time spent outside of Canada has no impact on whether or not the applicant is flagpoling.
3. What would happen if the applicant had urgent travel needs, and the purpose of their travels was not solely to access immigration services? E.g., urgent business travels.

When foreign nationals, who hold temporary resident status in Canada, leave Canada and after a visit to the United States or St. Pierre and Miquelon, re-enter for the purpose of obtaining immigration services at a port of entry including work and study permits they are considered to be flagpoling. If the applicant is visiting the U.S for work, but also intends to get a work permit upon their return at a port of entry, they would be considered to be obtaining immigration services, and therefore flagpoling unless they meet one of the exemptions. The applicant will not be able to obtain a work permit at the port of entry
éenvedsurlasomation no matter what reason they had for going to the U.S in the first place. In the event that CBSA is satisfied that the client in question is not ineligible to enter Canada as a visitor they could be issued a vistor record, resulting in the client losing their authorization to work in Canada until their original application for work permit extension is approved. Visitors are not eligible to apply for a work permit from inside Canada.
In exceptional circumstances, you can send an urgent work permit application (Urgent referrals process for work permits-Canada.ca) to IRCC if you are a:
- Doctor involved in the treatment of patients who is changing employers, moving to another province, or renewing their medical license,
or
- Worker who is travelling urgently due to business travel, or death or serious illness in the family.
4. If applicants under c) would be eligible to apply at the POE, what type of documentation should they present, if any, to demonstrate that their primary purpose of travel was not for immigration service?

Not applicable.
5. Would there be a difference if the applicant holds a valid work/study permit vs. travelling while under maintained status at the time of submitting the application at the port of entry.

If the applicant is flagpoling and is under maintained status at the time of submitting an application at a port of entry, they will lose their ability to work upon their return to Canada.

Thank you for sharing with us this information, we will also share it with CBSA for their awareness. Visitors cannot work and must wait until their original application for a work permit extension is approved.

Thank you for sharing with us this information, we will also share it with CBSA for their awareness. A foreign national would be flagpoling after a visit to the United States whether they were admitted to the United States or received an administrative refusal.

You can only apply at a port of entry if you're eligible. An officer would conduct an assessment of eligibility and admissibility at the port of entry based on the application being made at the time by the foreign national. Most foreign nationals in Canada can no longer apply for a work permit at a port of entry. You must apply online for your initial work permit and your work permit extension. If you leave Canada as a worker on maintained status, you'll lose your ability to work when you return. This means you can't work until your application is approved. threads.answer:
Good day,
Thank you for contacting the Immigration Represe ntatives Mailbox. Please note that this mailbox is intended for general guidance and does not provide responses to case-specific inquiries but have provided the following information as guidance. Ifyou have case specific questions about a file, you are encouraged to submit the IRCC Web form.
Please see our response to your question.
1. Can a holder of an Israeli Open Work Permit apply for an extension before the program closes, or is it a one-time permit only? Under the temporary measures for Israeli nationals, Palestinian passport holders and family members in Canada, eligible foreign nationals are able to apply for fee-exempt study permits, open work permits, or extensions of their temporary resident status in Canada. They are not limited to a single application under these temporary measures.
2. If extensions are permitted, can an applicant request one even if they still have two years remaining on their initial Israeli Open Work Permit? Applicants can request an extension under these special measures even if they still have time remaining on their initial open work permit as long as the application is made before the expiration of the public policy on July 31, 2025. Please note that when assessing an application for an extension, if significant duration remains on the client's current permit, the officer may take this factor into consideration before granting an extension.
3. If extensions are allowed, I assume the permit will be issued only up to the passport's expiry date. If the passport expires in less than three years, would it be possible to apply for the remaining validity period after the public policy has ended? Open work permits issued under the public policy may be issued for a maximum of 36 months or until the expiry of the applicant's passport or biometrics (whichever comes first) however, the validity period is always at the discretion of the officer. It is recommended that the applicant's passport be valid for a longer period than the requested extension before applying. If the applicant's passport expires in less than three years, it would not be possible to apply for the potential remaining validity period after the public policy has ended. The applicant would need to apply to extend or change the conditions of their work permit under regular processes, outlined here. - And if so, if their visitor's record reflects allowed to work online without requiring a work permit while in Canada, can their spouses apply for an open WP as the dependent of a high skilled worker? Similarly to exemptions under R186?
RESPONSE:
- Foreign nationals seeking entry to Canada as a visitor and whose intent is to be a digital nomad do not have to request a visitor record from the Canadian Border Services Agency (CBSA) at a port of entry, unless they wish to do so. If a visitor record is requested, there will be no difference between what is issued if the individual is coming as a digital nomad, or if their intent in visiting Canada is for any other temporary stay of 6 months. Information on issuing visitor records by either CBSA or IRCC can be found here.
- Family members of someone coming to work in Canada as a digital nomad cannot apply for an open work permit as the dependent of a high skilled worker. They can apply for a work permit, if eligible, on their own.

threads.answer:

Question:
Medical doctors who hold an employer-specific work permit working in a hospital are sometimes asked to supervise and train medical students on behalf of a university, in the course of their work at the hospital
In order for the university to provide an appointment to the doctor, is a separate work permit required (with the university listed as the employer) if

Respons e: Thank you for your inquiry. In both cases, whether the university is providing payment to the doctor or not, a separate work permit is not required as long as the doctor meets the eligibility criteria outlined for medical residents or medical fellowship holders.
The work permit issued under the employer-specific category covers their duties, whether they involve supervising and training medical students or conducting clinical or research work. They must also be offered a residency position that is not publicly funded in Canada.
For medical fellowship holders, eligibility requires holding a medical degree equivalent to that of a Canadian Medical Doctorate (MD), being a recognized medical specialist who has completed residency training, and accepting to continue specializing in a highly specific field of study to advance clinical or medical research.

Question:

Protected persons are exempt from requiring a provincial attestation letter. Protected persons include convention refugees and persons in need of protection. Therefore, convention refugees do not require a provincial attestation letter.
A refugee claimant will receive a conditional Removal Order. With a conditional removal order, the removal order does not come into force under A49(2) until specific events have passed. At the time the removal order is made, it is not in force and is conditional until it comes into force on the latest of the following dates:
the day the claim is determined to be ineligible under A101(1)(e) if the claimant came directly or indirectly to Canada from a country designated by the Regulations, other than a country of their nationality or former habitual residence [A49(2)(a)];
in all cases other than A101(1)(e), seven days after the claim is determined to be ineligible [A49(2)(b)]; or
15 days after notification that the claim has been rejected

threads.subject: Supervisa --REP-2024-0480
threads.question:
Dear ImmReps,
We are seeing a consistent issue with supervisa entrants to Canada if they are from visa exempt countries. Your website provides that when approved applicants arrive in Canada, they will present the documents used for the supervisa application to the officer, and their passport will be stamped allowing them to stay for 5 years.
Have your documents ready
When you arrive, you'll be greeted by an officer from the Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA).
3The officer will ask to see your passport or travel documents. You should also bring the documents you used for your super visa application (opens in a new tab). Make sure these documents aren't packed in your luggage.
A valid super visa and travel document (passport, titre de voyage or Certificate of Identity) does not guarantee that you can enter Canada.
You enter Canada
Ifyou pass the identity check and meet the entry requirements, the border services officer will stamp your passport, allowing you to stay in Canada for 5 years.
You won't be allowed into Canada if you give false or incomplete information. You must convince the officer that
- you're eligible for entry into Canada
- you'll leave Canada at the end of your approved stay
This doesn't happen in practice. In the majority of cases, their passports are not stamped. We had one client enter yesterday from the UK. All the documents used for the supervisa application including the approval letter were presented to the officer. The officer advised that they were from a visa exempt country and could come and go with an ETA. The officer did not stamp the passport.
Normally, if a passport isn't stamped, we assume the applicant can stay for six months. What is IRCC’s position on this issue? Do we now have to apply for a Visitor Record to confirm that the applicant can stay for 5 years if the passport wasn't stamped? If so, why should an applicant pay another $100 processing fee if CBSA isn't providing the required stamp?
Or, can we assume they can stay for 5 years on the basis of having a supervisa approval letter and proof of entry (i.e. flight itinerary).?
Thank you for your attention to this matter.
threads.answer:
Immigration Representatives / Représentants inmigration (IRCC)
Good afternoon,
Thank you for your email correspondence to 's Immigration Representatives mailbox.
QUESTION
We are seeing a consistent issue with supervisa entrants to Canada if they are from visa exempt countries. Your website provides that when approved applicants arrive in Canada, they will present the documents used for the supervisa application to the officer, and their passport will be stamped allowing them to stay for 5 years.
This doesn't happen in practice. In the majority of cases, their passports are not stamped. We had one client enter yesterday from the UK. All the documents used for the supervisa application including the approval letter were presented to the officer. The officer advised that they were from a visa exempt country and could come and go with an ETA. The officer did not stamp the passport.
Normally, if a passport isn't stamped, we assume the applicant can stay for six months. What is IRCC's position on this issue? Do we now have to apply for a Visitor Record to confirm that the applicant can stay for 5 years if the passport wasn't stamped? If so, why should an applicant pay another $100 processing fee if CBSA isn't providing the required stamp?
Or, can we assume they can stay for 5 years on the basis of having a supervisa approval letter and proof of entry (i.e. flight itinerary)?
ANSWER
This information is provided as general policy guidance and is not a directive for individual case files. For case specific enquiries, applicants can contact the Department by submitting the IRCC Web form.
Foreign nationals from visa-exempt countries generally require an electronic travel authorization (eTA) to travel to Canada. If their super visa application is approved, these individuals will be issued a super visa port of entry (POE) letter, rather than a visa counterfoil in their passport. They will need to apply separately for an eTA if they do not already have one.
If parents and grandparents who possess the temporary resident super visa or letter of introduction have a stamp in their passport with no handwritten date, or if they have no stamp, then the period of authorized stay is 5 years from the date of entry.
Consult Examination and entry (tenporary residents) for more information.
Please note that it is important for Super Visa holders to ensure that their passport as well as their health insurance remain valid
Citoyenneté Canada
for the duration of their stay in Canada.

Thank you kindly,

X has been offered employment at Company Y as a Mining Engineer. The employment location is in Toronto. The prevailing wage for Mining Engineers in Toronto is $46/hour. X’s guaranteed/hourly salary is $42/hour; however, per the offer of employment, he is entitled to get 25 percent of his salary as a guaranteed bonus notwithstanding his performance or company’s yearly profit. This bonus structure increases his guaranteed income to just over $50/hourly. In this case, with the addition of the guaranteed bonus, X’s wage will exceed the current prevailing wage.

- overtime hours
- tips
- benefits
- profit sharing
- bonuses
- commissions
- other forms of compensation

Thank you for you attention to this matter.

Par conséquent, si l’enfant à charge se marie ou s’engage dans une union de fait après la soumission de l’application, il ne répondra désormais plus à la définition d’enfant à charge et ne sera donc pas admissible à un visa de résident permanent, que son état matrimonial redevienne ou non celui de célibataire, divorcé ou mariage annulé. Le bureau des visas doit être informé de tout changement de circonstances, y compris lorsque l’état civil d’un enfant à charge a changé.
L'alinéa 40(1)a) de la Loi sur l’immigration et la protection des réfugiés (LIPR) stipule que :
\cbpat3« directement ou indirectement, faire une présentation erronée sur un fait important quant à un objet pertinent, ou une réticence sur ce fait, ce qui entraîne ou risque d’entraîner une erreur dans l’application de la présente loi »
Donc, directement ou indirectement faire de fausse déclaration ou dissimuler des faits, tel que l’état matrimonial d’un enfant à charge, constitue une fausse déclaration sous l’article 40(1)(a) du RIPR et peut entrainer une interdiction de territoire pour une période de cinq ans. En outre, une personne à charge non contrôlée, y compris un époux ou un conjoint de fait qui n’a pas été déclarée ou n’a pas fait l’objet d’un contrôle, est considérée une relation exclue et ne sera donc pas éligible à un parrainage futur, conformément à la directive de l’article R125(1)(d).

threads.subject: working off campus for visiting research students -- REP-2024-0547 --
threads.question:
Hello.
I would like to clarify an off-campus work authorization for visiting research students who hold a valid study permit wit h the work authorization (on and off campus).
These students are full-time enrolled students in a DLI for 6 mont hs or more, but their program does not lead them to a degree in the DLl, as they are visiting researchers from their home institutions.
My question is, do they meet all the crit eria to work off-campus according to policy here? Or are they limited to work on-campus only because their studies here do not lead to a degree or diploma here.
Thank you for your time.
mmigration, Refugees mmigration, Réfugiés
threads.answer:
Thank you for your inquiry.
International students with a valid study permit may work off campus without a work permit if they meet all of the following eligibility re quire ments :
- They are a full-time student at a designated learning institution (DLI)
- They are enrolled in either of the following o a post-secondary academic, vocational or professional training program or a secondary-level vocational training program (Quebec only)
- their study program is at least 6 months long and leads to a degree, diploma or certificate
- they started studying
- they have a social insurance number (SIN)
Ineligible programs of study
Students are not eligible for the off-campus work permit program if either of the following applies:
- they are registered in a general interest program of study that does not meet the definition of an academic, professional or vocational training program as defined above (for instance, ESL/FSL courses for self-improvement)
- they are undertaking a course or program of study that is a prerequisite to their enrolment at a DLI
Students who are enrolled in a program of study that meets the definition of an academic, professional or vocational training program and who are undertaking the ESL/FSL component simultaneously may be eligible to work off campus pursuant to paragraph R186(v) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR).
Therefore, if a student has a one semester exchange study that is at least 6 months long and meets all of the other requirements mentioned above, they are eligible to work off campus during their semester exchange.
Please visit Work off campus as an international student-Canada.ca for additional information.
We hope this information has been helpful.

threads.question: Subject: Questions regarding COOP for international students Dear team, I hope this email finds you well. I had a question regarding COOP for international students. I wanted to ask can the COOP be part time? How many hours of work per week are considered as a full time work experience for COOP? And how many hours are considered as part-time? If the COOP can be part-time, can the student work in COOP job for lets say 20 hours/week and also take 1 course alongside and still be considered a full time student? Or is there a certain number of courses to be taken along with part time COOP to be considered a full time student? I respectfully thank you in advance for your help. I look forward to hearing from you soon. Thanks and Regards,
threads.answer:
Hello Thank you for your inquiry. Question 1. Can the COOP be part time? Respons e 1. There are no regulations that specify the number of hours of co-op or internship program employment. However, the following conditions must be met:
- the student must have a valid study permit and their intended employment must be o an essential part of a postsecondary academic, vocational or professional training program; o an essential part of a vocational training program at the secondary level in Quebec; or o an essential part of a secondary level program that requires student to work in order to obtain their secondary or high school diploma or certificate of graduation, 。 offered by a DLI.
- The intended employment must be certified as part of the academic program by a responsible academic official of the DLI; and
- the co-op or internship employment cannot form more than 50 percent of the total program of study; and
- the student is not a medical intern or extern, nor a resident physician (except in veterinary medicine).
Question 2. How many hours of work per week are considered as a full time work experience for COOP? And how many hours are considered as part-time? Response 2. As per section 73(1) of the IRPR, full-time work means at least 30 hours of work over a period of one week. Part-time work therefore means less than 30 hours.
While the co-op work cannot form more than 50 percent of the total program of study, there is no set number of“full time" hours per week specific to co-op or internship employment. However, the employer(s) must follow all provincial laws on overtime pay and time between shifts.
Question 3. If the COOP can be part-time, can the student work in COOP job for lets say 20 hours/week and also take 1 course alongside and still be considered a full time student? Or is there a certain number of courses to be taken along with part time COOP to be considered a full time student? Response 3. Although the definition of full-time or part-time studies may vary depending on the educational institution, full-time is defined in section 102.2(1) of the IRPR as requiring at least 15 hours of instruction per week during the academic year, including any period of training in the workplace that forms part of the course of instruction. Note that, except for the province of Quebec, which requires students to maintain full-time status with their institution to be considered to be actively pursuing their studies, study permits may be issued whether or not the student’s studies are on a full-time or part-time basis, as long as they are enrolled at a designated learning institution. However, the student must have a full-time status in order to work on or off campus. Different requirements apply to on or off campus work that is not an essential part of a of an academic, professional or vocational training program (i.e., not a co-op or internship program).

Immgration Kepresentatves / Representants inmigration (IRCC)
Good morning,
Please find the response to your inquiry below.
Question: Our team has a question about the temporary public policy allowing temporary workers to study without a study permit.
For Temporary Workers who study without a study permit for part of a program, and obtain a study permit to cover the remainder of their studies after their work permit expires-- are they eligible to apply for the Post-Graduation Work Permit (PGWP)? Would the length of PGWP include the length of the program they studied under the work permit?
For example, student studies 6 months of a 1-year program under the work permit, and the final 6 months under a study permit
Response: Thank you for your inquiry. Temporary workers who study without a study permit for part of a program and later obtain a study permit to continue their studies after their work permit expires are eligible to apply for the Post-Graduation Work Permit (PGWP).
However, it's important to note that the length of the PGWP would not include the duration of the program they studied under the work permit. The eligibility criteria for the PGWP require that the individual completes a full program of study at a designated learning institution (DLI) in Canada. Since the time spent studying under the work permit wouldn't count towards fulflling this requirement, it would not be included in the calculation of the PGWP duration.
In the example provided, if a student studies 6 months of a 1-year program under the work permit and completes the remaining 6 months under a study permit, only the duration of the program completed under the study permit would be considered for the PGWP eligibility. Therefore, in this case, the PGWP duration would be based on the 6 months of study completed under the study permit.

threads.answer:
Good day,
Thank you for your questions.
In the case of an overseas humanitarian and compassionate (H&C) application, applicants must apply under one of the three immigration classes (fanily, economic or refugee) using the corresponding departmental application forimns for the class under which they are applying. Applicants must then also provide additional written information in support of their request for consideration under subsection A25(1). Permanent resident visa applicants who do not meet the applicable criteria or obligations of the immigration class they are applying under and wish for H&C grounds to be considered must provide additional written information in support of their request for consideration under subsection A25(1). Applicants are free to make submissions on any aspect of their personal circumstances that they believe are relevant to their request for H&C consideration. The applicant bears the onus of satisfying the decision maker that the H&C factors and their individual circumstances are sufficient to warrant the exemption(s) requested. Requests for H&C consideration are reviewed on a case-by-case basis. The H&C decision-making process is highly discretionary. The decision maker considers whether a special grant of an exemption from the requirements of the Act is warranted. Invoking sections A25 and A25.1 is an exceptional measure and not simply an alternate means of applying for permanent resident status in Canada.
If a positive H&C decision is made, the applicant must still satisfy the remaining requirements for a permanent resident visa including medical, criminal records checks and security screening. Once all requirements are met, a permanent resident visa may be issued.
Thank you,

Question
J'ai une question concernant le PTPD. Si un étudiant a suivi un programme DEP de 1450 heures qui se termine en août 2024, et qu'il prévoit de suivre un ASP commençant en décembre 2024, ce qui, combiné au DEP, totalise plus de 1800 heures, tous deux dans des écoles désignées. Le DEP était entièrement en présentiel, tandis que l'ASP est entièrement en ligne. Est-ce que cela pourrait poser problème lors de la demande de permis de travail post-diplôme, même si plus de 50% de la durée totale des deux programmes combinés est en présentiel ? Doit-il justifier qu'elle a complété 50% de chaque programme en présentiel ou des deux combinés ?
Veuillez consulter notre réponse à vos questions ci-dessous.
Réponse
Conformément aux instructions, un officier peut combiner les cours suivis par un étudiant en considérant son programme d’études global. Par conséquent, tant que 50% du temps total d’étude était consacré à l’enseignement en face à face le demandeur peut peut-être admissible à un PTPD.
Études au Canada
- Jusquau 31 août 2024 vous devez compléter au moins 50% de votre programme en ligne ou en classe au Canada.
- À compter du 1er septembre 2024, vous devez réaliser au moins 50% de votre programme en classe au Canada.
Veuillez noter que la méthode d’enseignement ne s’agit qu’une des mesures envisagées et que le demandeur doit conformer à tous les instructions du Ministre afin d’être admissible au PTPD.
Prenez attention aux instructions suivantes quant au cumul des programmes :
Cumul des programmnes
Jusqu’au 31 août 2024, les étudiants admissibles qui terminent 2 programmes d’études admissibles, où les 2 programmes étaient en cours en mars 2020 ou ont commencé entre mars 2020 et le 31 août 2022, pourraient être en mesure de :
- terminer la totalité des 2 progranmes à l’extérieur du Canada (si les 2 programmes étaient en cours en mars 2020 ou commencés entre
mars 2020 et le 31 août 2022);
- combiner la durée de leurs programmes d’études lorsqu’ils présenteront une éventuelle demande de PTPD.
Selon les instructions actuelles sur la détermination de la durée du PTPD, les 2 progranmes doivent être :
- d’une durée d’au moins 8 mois;
- terminé dans un EED admissible à l’intérieur de 2 ans.
Les étudiants qui ont commencé leur deuxième programme le 1er septembre 2022 ou après ne sont pas admissibles à la mesure spéciale, même si leur premier programme était en cours en mars 2020 ou a commencé entre mars 2020 et le 31 août 2022.
Remarque : Pour les étudiants qui suivent des programmes de formation professionnelle au Québec, le programme de diplôme d’études professionnelles

threads.answer:
Hello,
Please see our response to your question.
QUESTION:
Currently, my client is employed under her RNIP Work Permit, which is due to expire in September 2024. She is uncertain if it is necessary to extend her Work Permit upon expiration. The IRCC website does not provide detailed information on how to extend an RNIP Work Permit, which is why we are seeking your guidance.
Could you please clarify if an RNIP Applicant is required to maintain a Work Permit and continue working in Canada while awaiting the outcome of their PR Application? Their PR Application is currently undergoing a comprehensive security check which may be quite lengthy. If holding a Work Permit and working in Canada is not a requirement for RNIP, my client may consider extending her status as a visitor within Canada.
Could you please kindly confirm if there is a procedure for extending the RNIP Work Permit, and if RNIP Applicants are allowed to hold a Visitor Record in Canada while waiting for their PR Application outcome?
RESPONSE:
If someone has applied under RNIP for permanent residence (PR), they may be eligible for an optional 1-year work permit. This work permit lets the individual work in Canada while IRCC processes their PR application. To qualify for this type of work permit, the individual must have the following
- an eligible offer of employment from your employer
- a recommendation from a participating community
- be eligible to apply for a work permit
- have received an acknowledgement of receipt letter from us
RNIP applicants who require additional time in Canada while their PR application is being processed may apply to extend their work permit. If they want to extend their work permit, they will need the above-noted documents (e.g., offer or employment; recommendation from a participating community, the acknowledgement of receipt for their permanent residence application) in order to apply for an extension.
When it comes to the RNIP work permit, as noted above, this is optional. If the individual wants to remain in Canada while IRCC processes their PR application, they can apply for a visitor visa. Please note that if they let their temporary resident status expire, they will need to leave Canada and wait for a decision on their PR application from outside of Canada. Temporary residents (e.g., international students, temporary foreign workers, visitors) must maintain their status at all times while in Canada.

threads.answer:
Hello,
Thank you for your enquiry concerning the work experience requirements for the Agri-Food Pilot.
In order for Canadian work experience to be eligible under the Agri-Food Pilot, it must be:
at least 1 year of cumulative, non-seasonal, full-time work in the past 3 years (at least 1,560 hours)
in 1 or more of the eligible occupations listed under 1 of the eligible industries
gained though
o an open work permit for vulnerable workers or
o a work permit issued on the basis of a labour market impact assessment (LMIA) with a minimum 12-month duration, under the Temporary Foreign Worker Prograim
As the work experience requirement is 1 year of cumulative full-time work in the past 3 years, the 12 months of experience can be split between different eligible work permits. The work permits under which an applicant can show eligible work experience for the AFP is an open work permit for vulnerable workers (O WP-V), or a work permit issued on a minimumn 12 month LMIA under the TFWP.
For your question specifically, the eligibility of the applicant's work experience would depend on whether the open work permit on which they worked for 7 months was specifically an open work permnit for vulnerable workers. An OWP-V is the only kind of open work permit through which an applicant can acquire eligible work experience under the pilot. If the client worked for 7 months on an OWP-V, followed by 10 months on an LMIA work permit valid for 24 months, this would be considered meeting the 12 months of eligible work experience requirement. However, if the 7 months was on any kind of open work permit other than the OWP-V, this period of work experience would not count, and the applicant would need to gain 2 more months of eligible work experience to apply.

Is admission to the USA under s. 207 of the American Immigration & Nationality Act considered a Durable Solution that would exclude an asylum-seeker from refugee resettlement under s. 139(1)(d) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations? threads.answer:
Imnigration Representatives / Représentants inmigration (IRCC)
Hi,
[n Canadian programs, the term“asylum-seeker" is normally reserved for refugee protection claimants at POEs or inside Canada. It is assumed here that the requester is talking about refugee resettlement from abroad.
After review of open-source material from the USCIS website, the general refugee resettlement process in the US appears similar to Canada’s process with one major difference: resettled refugees do not become permanent residents upon landing. They must apply for PR status after one year, which means that in the interim, they hold “refugee” status only, similar to what port of entry and in-Canada asylum claimants have upon approval of their claim.
US applicants hold refugee status (which is neither temporary resident nor permanent resident status) from the time they are admitted to the US until they become permanent resident after submitting an application. Denial of this PR application on inadmissibility may place the refugee into removal proceedings, provided there are applicable grounds of deportability. For other grounds of denial, the applicant continues to have refugee status and may renew the application for PR.
Refugees in the US may travel abroad provided they obtain a Refugee Travel Document in advance of their departure in order to return to the US.
3ased on this, on current published IRCC guidance regarding durable solution and pursuant to section 139(1)(d) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations, the situation you are describing may qualify as “resettlement or an offer of resettlement to a country (other than Canada)" and may result in a refusal of the application with IRCC.

As indicated on our website regarding the education requirements for the Home Support Worker pilot, an applicant must provide evidence that they have either of the following completed in order to apply: a Canadian one-year post-secondary educational credential or a foreign educational credential and an Educational Credential Assessment (ECA) report issued by an organization designated by IRCC.

threads.question:
Hello,
We have been directed to you for help in clarifying the new field of study requirement for PGwP eligibility based on the following scenarios:
●* Scenario 1: Student arrived in Canada to start Program A in September 2024. Upon arriving, they realized the program was not a good fit and transitioned to Program B (not meeting PGWP field of study requirement) in September 2024. They were issued a Letter of Acceptance for Program B in September 2024. if they require a Study Permit extension in the future for Program B, are they eligible for the PGWP without meeting the Field of Study Requirements?
- * Scenario 2: Student applies for a Study Permit using a conditional Letter of Acceptance for ESL + Program C (not meeting PGWP field of study requirement) in September 2024. The condition is 4 levels of ESL courses at our institution, which will be completed by May 2025. Their original study permit will not cover the length of Program C. They will receive a non-conditional Letter of Acceptance to Program C after completing the required levels of ESL. Are they eligible for the PGWP without meeting the Field of Study Requirements?
- * Scenario 3: Student arrived in Canada to start Program 1 (not meeting PGWP field of study requirement) in January 2024. They start Program 2 (not meeting PĠWP field of study requirement) in January 2025. Their study permit was issued from January 2024 until December 2025. They do not need to extend their study permit at any time before completing Program 2. Are they eligible for the PGWP without meeting the Field of Study Requirements for both programs because no study permit extension needs to be submitted after November 1, 2024?
- * Scenario 4: Student applied for their initial study permit with a letter of acceptance for DLl-A. Student completed one semester of original program at DLl-A in September 2023 and then changed their program (not meeting PGWP field of study requirement) and started studying at DLI-B in January 2024. Student will need to extend their study permit in May 2025 to complete program at DLl-B. Is the program at DLI-B considered a current program or a new program and will they be eligible for a PĠwP?
Thank you so much for your feedback on these scenarios.
Kind regards,
threads.answer:
Good day, Thank you for contacting the Immigration Represe ntatives Mailbox. Please note that this mailbox is intended for general guidance and does not provide responses to case-specific inquiries but have provided the following information as guidance. If you have case specific questions about a file, you are encouraged to submit the IRCC Web form. Please see our response to your question. ***
Scenario 1: Student arrived in Canada to start Program A in September 2024. Upon arriving, they realized the program was not a good fit and transitioned to Program B (not meeting PGWP field of study requirement) in September 2024. They were issued a Letter of Acceptance for Program B in September 2024. If they require a Study Permit extension in the future for Program B, are they eligible for the PGWP without meeting the Field of Study Requirements?
RESPONSE:
If the student applies for a study permit extension under the same program for which they have study authorization via the study permit they applied for before November 1, 2024, then they do not need to meet the field of study requirement. If the student applies for a study permit extension under a different program than the study permit they applied for before November 1, 2024, then their study permit extension application must meet the field of study requirements applicable to their study program to be eligible for a PGWP.
Scenario 2: Student applies for a Study Permit using a conditional Letter of Acceptance for ESL + Program C (not meeting PGWP field of study requirement) in September 2024. The condition is 4 levels of ESL courses at our institution, which will be completed by May 2025. Their original study permit will not cover the length of Program C. They will receive a non-conditional Letter of Acceptance to Program C after completing the required levels of ESL. Are they eligible for the PGWP without meeting the Field of Study Requirements?
RESPONSE:
Please see response to scenario 1. If the student applied for the original study permit before November 1, 2024, and subsequently apply for a study permit extension to continue Program C, they would be applying under the same program of study and therefore not subject to the field of study requirement.
Scenario 3: Student arrived in Canada to start Program 1 (not meeting PGWP field of study requirement) in January
2024. They start Program 2 (not meeting PGWP field of study requirement) in January 2025. Their study permit was issued from January 2024 until December 2025. They do not need to extend their study permit at any time before completing Program 2. Are they eligible for the PGWP without meeting the Field of Study Requirements for both programs because no study permit extension needs to be submitted after November 1, 2024? RESPONSE: If a student completes two consecutive programs that are PGwP-eligible within two years of completion of the first program when applying for a PGWP, both programs could be considered for the purpose of determining the length of
the PGWP.
To qualify for program stacking in relation to PGWP duration, both PGWP-eligible programs must be:
* a minimum of 8 months in duration; and
- * completed at a PGWP-eligible DLl within 2 years of the completion of the first program.
In determining whether a program is PGWP-eligible, the field of study requirement is applicable depending on the level of study and when a student applies for their study permit (see response to Scenario 1). If the student applied for both study permits to pursue Programs 1 and 2 before November 1, 2024, then the field of study requirement does not apply. If the student applies for their study permit for Program 2 on or after November 1, 2024, then this program would need to meet the field of study requirement to be considered a PGWP-eligible program.
If only Program 1 is PGWP-eligible, the student must apply for their PGWP within 180 days of receiving written confirmation of completing this program, in addition to all other requirements, to be eligible for a PGWP based on Program 1.
Scenario 4: Student applied for their initial study permit with a letter of acceptance for DLl-A Student completed one semester of original program at DLl-A in September 2023 and then changed their program (not meeting PGWP field of study requirement) and started studying at DLi-B in January 2024. Student will need to extend their study permit in May 2025 to complete program at DLl-B. Is the program at DLi-B considered a current program or a new program and will they be eligible for a PGWP ?
RESPONSE:
If the student's initial study permit gives them study authorization for the program at DLl-B and they applied for this permit before November 1, 2024, then this would be an extension of their current program and the field of study requirement does not apply (noting the study permit issued for their extension application would indicate the information for DLI-B).
Please note, as of November 8, 2024, section 217.1 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations, study permit holders in Canada, whose permit names a DLl, must apply for a new study permit if they wish to change DLls. If the officer determines that a PGWP applicant did not meet the conditions of their study permit, they may be prohibited from being issued a work permit for 6 months from the date they stopped their unauthorized study or work, as per subparagraph R200(3)(e)(i).
For more information, please see our updated PGWP guidance for clients: Work or live in Canada after you graduate-Canada.ca
We hope this information is of assistance.
Thank you kindly,

Please see our response to your question. *** First, it is important to highlight the comparison raised in your email between 'expungement' and ‘automatic conviction record relief' under California Penal Code 1203.425:
- * Expunge typically refers to the action of erasing or removing entirely. It is our understanding in the context of United States law, an “expungement” is the process by which a record of criminal conviction is destroyed or sealed from state or federal record. As such, this would mean that the court treats the criminal conviction as if it had never occurred, essentially removing it from a client's criminal record.
- * If and when relief is granted pursuant to the aforementioned penal code, the state summary criminal history information shall include a note to the effect of “relief granted." It is our understanding, this note shall be included in statewide criminal databases with a record of the conviction noted therein. Thus, it seems automatic conviction record relief, pursuant to California Penal Code 1203.425, does not result in the removal of the criminal record in its entirety, but rather, results in the amendment of the respective client's criminal record to formally document and reflect that relief has been granted.
- * Should there exist a subsequent prosecution of the client for any other offence, it is further understood that the prior conviction may be pleaded and proved, and shall have the same effect as if the relief, formerly granted pursuant to the aforementioned penal code, had not been granted.
Secondly, in terms of how IRCC treats convictions that have a notation for automatic relief under California Penal Code
1203.425, the legislative parameters for a criminal inadmissibility within the context of Canadian immigration/permanent resident matters, is outlined in subsections 36(1), 36(2), and 36(2.1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA). It is important to note, that per paragraph 36(3)(c) of IRPA, a criminal inadmissibility finding may not be based on a conviction in respect of which a record suspension has been ordered and has not been revoked or ceased to have effect under the Criminal
Records Act.

California Penal Code 1203.425 satisfies the provision(s) noted under 36(3)(c) of IRPA.

Your institution sent the student a letter of admission, but they are no longer registered or enrolled because they have
* been dismissed

threads.subject: Début du calcul d'une union de fait aux fins de 28 LIPR-REP-B-2025-0298 - 7-May-25
threads.question:
Bonjour,
J’espère que vous allez bien.
Je m’adresse à vous concernant la question suivante, car je ne parviens pas à trouver de réponse dans les directives d’IRCC ou la législation. « Lorsque nous invoquons une exception à 28 LIPR pour l'obligation de présence effective parce que le résident permanent est en union de fait avec un Canadien et vivent tous deux à l'étranger, le début du calcul de l'union de fait débute-t-il à la date de début de cohabitation Ou dès que cela fait 12 mois et un jour qu'ils cohabitent? » Par exemple, une personne est résidente permanente et cohabite avec son conjoint canadien dans un pays X depuis septembre 2023. Dans ce pays X, ils sont considérés en union de fait dès qu'ils débutent la cohabitation (donc septembre
2023). IRCC compterait-il également le début de l’union de fait en septembre 2023 ou plutôt septembre 2024? C'est déterminant pour connaitre le nombre de jours qui pourraient être comptabilisés comme "étant au Canada" pour cette personne. En vous remerciant, je vous souhaite une belle journée. Meilleures salutations,
threads.answer:
Bonjour,
Merci d’avoir contacté la boîte aux courriels pour les représentants en immigration. Veuillez noter que cette boîte aux lettres est destinée à fournir des conseils généraux et ne fournit pas de réponses à des demandes spécifiques à un cas, mais a fourni les informations suivantes comme conseil. Si vous avez des questions spécifiques à un dossier, nous vous encourageons à soumettre le formulaire Formulaire Web d'IRCC-Canada.ca Veuillez consulter notre réponse à votre question.
À propos du conjoint de fait : Pour être considéré conjoints de fait, les individus doivent avoir continuellement cohabités pour au moins une année. Cette définition est utilisée comme un standard dans toutes les institutions fédérales, et est cohérente avecla définition de conjoint de fait des RIPR sous R1(1).
À propos de l’obligation de résidence A28: A28(2)(a)(ii) « il accompagne, hors du Canada, un citoyen canadien qui est son époux ou conjoint de fait... », est interprété comme suit : la personne doit déjà être dans une relation de conjoint de fait à leur départ du Canada alors qu’elle accompagne le citoyen canadien hors du Canada. Cette interprétation a été défendu devant la Division d’appels en immigration (DAl); et la jurisprudence à ce sujet indique que le parlement avait l’intention que A28(2)(a)(ii) serve de filet de sureté pour les résidents permanents quittant le Canada afin d’être avecleurs époux ou leurs conjoints de fait citoyen canadien (et non-pas résidents permanents, hors du Canada, et qui deviennent par la suite l’époux d’un citoyen canadien).
- * A61(4) met aussi l’emphase sur le fait que l’individu déjà en union de fait « ... le résident permanent accompagne hors du Canada un citoyen canadien ou un résident permanent — gui est son époux ou conjoint de fait ou, dans le cas d’un enfant, l’un de ses parents — chaque jour où il réside habituellement avec lui. »
- * En général, la DAi se fie sur la définition de « accompagner » en tant que verbe demandant au sujet (le résident permanent) de prendre certaines actions envers l’objet (leur époux ou conjoint de fait citoyen canadien) tel que chercher à être ensemble, suivre et/ou escorter.
Ce qui veut dire : En prenant ces éléments en considération, 3 scénarios peuvent se produire :
●* Si le couple est déjà en union de fait avant leur départ du Canada, alors le calcul selon A28 tiendrait chaque jour où le résident permanent réside ordinairement avecle citoyen canadien. •* Si le couple cohabitait pour une période de moins d'un an avant leur départ du Canada et que les partenaires deviennent des conjoints de fait à l’étranger, la question revient à savoir quand et comment ils seront considérés comme « accompagnant » le conjoint de fait à l’étranger. Les décideurs devront déterminer selon l’information qui leur a été fourni, et s’ils sont satisfaits que le résident permanent « accompagne » bel et bien son conjoint de fait à l’extérieur du Canada. Les décideurs peuvent utiliser leurs pouvoirs discrétionnaires pour toutes considérations d’ordre humanitaires (H&C).
- * Si le couple n’a jamais cohabité au Canada, la jurisprudence de la DAl semble pencher pour que ce type de cas, le couple ne rencontrerait pas la définition de « accompagner un conjoint de fait hors du Canada. »
Nous espérons que vous trouviez ces informations utiles.
and Cizenship Caneda
*** Cordialement, La boîte aux courriels pour les représentants en immigration

Dear Rep Mailbox,
Dear IRCC Representative,
I am seeking clarification regarding the eligibility of job offers under the upcoming Home Care Worker Immigration Pilots set to launch on March 31, 2025. Specifically, I want to confirm whether a job offer from a direct care agency or home health care service provider is valid under the pilot.
Key Questions:
1. 1. Employment Relationship:
o* If a direct care agency or home health care provider directly employs a caregiver (issues payroll, benefits, and a T4) and assigns them to a private household, would this be considered an eligible job offer for the pilot?
2. 2. Payment Structure:
o* If a private household pays the agency directly, and the agency then pays the caregiver as a full-time employee, does this meet the job offer requirements for the pilot?
3. 3. Exclusion of Placement/Recruitment Agencies:
o * The pilot states that recruitment and placement agencies are not eligible employers. Can IRCC confirm the criteria used to distinguish between:
■* An eligible home care agency that directly employs caregivers and places them in private homes (acting
as the caregiver's official employer)?
■* An ineligible recruitment or placement agency that merely connects caregivers with private households
but does not officially employ them?
4. 4. Caregiver Work Location & Elderly Care Facilities:
o* The pilot specifies that home care workers must work in private homes. o* If a caregiver is employed by a long-term care home, nursing home, or assisted living facility, would this job offer be ineligible under the pilot? o * Are there any exceptions for caregivers working in residential care settings (e.g., group homes for individuals with disabilities) where they provide personal home-like care?
5. 5. Caregiver Education Credential-in the past CAREGIVER PILOT, 6-months courses for Caregiver and HSWP were sufficient. We did not need ECA for this. Is this eligible for this pilot? Is it important if it is in person or online?
I would greatly appreciate your clarification on these points, which would ensure that applicants and employers understand the correct eligibility requirements before the pilot launches.
Regards,
threads.answer:
Good Day,
Thank you for contacting the Immigration Representative Mailbox. Please note the Home Care Worker Immigration pilots are full for 2025.
To qualify for the Home Care Worker Immigration pilots, applicants must have a genuine job offer as home child care provider or home support worker, depending on which pilot they apply for, from an employer that is either a private household or business that provides direct care services in a private residence.
Job offers from direct care agencies may be eligible, but it depends on the specific nature of the caregiving role and employer-employee relationship. If the caregiving work involves providing personal care services in a residential setting and the employer directly hires, controls working conditions and remunerates the foreign national, the job offer may qualify. Officers will use all available information to determine whether the applicant will be providing services that align with the NOC and whether the work setting is considered the care recipient's private residence. Please see here for eligible employers.
As stated on the website: The job must be:
* in the National Occupational Classification (NOC) of the pilot you apply for: o* Home Care Worker Immigration Pilot: Child Care
* Home child care providers (NOC 44100) ■* The location can't be an institutional setting such as a daycare.
* A job as a foster parent doesn't count.
o * Home Care Worker Immigration Pilot: Home Support
* Home support workers, caregivers and related occupations (NOC 44101)
* The location can't be an institutional setting such as a nursing home.
To meet the educational requirement, applicants must have completed the equivalent of a Canadian high school diploma or higher. If they completed their education outside Canada, they'll need to get their education credential assessed to show that it's equal to a Canadian high school diploma (or higher).
To qualify under the Home Care Worker Immigration pilots, applicants must have enough relevant work experience OR training.
Applicants must have either 6 months of continuous, full-time and relevant work experience in the past 3 years OR completed relevant training that was at least 6 months in length, resulted in a post-secondary diploma, certificate or credential, and was completed in the past 2 years before they apply. The training must also be offered mainly in an in-person classroom environment.
An education credential is not required for the training credential, but is required to demonstrate the client has met or exceeded the education requirement (noted above). If an applicant's education credential also meets the conditions of the training requirement, the same credential may be applied to both the education and training requirements.
The work experience or training needs to correspond to the occupation that the applicant is applying to. We trust this information will assist you.
Thank you kindly,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.subject: Query; work on implied status while applying visitor record within restoration-REP-B-2025-0425 - Due 20-
threads.question:
Good day Team IRCC, Please assist me with the following query.
1*and Citizenshi Canada et Ciloyeneé Canada
Question: If an applicant is currently on implied status with an on-going Work Permit extension Application and hasn't received a decision yet also filed for a visitor record while in restoration period and is still under processing for both application(s), can he/she continue to work until a decision has been made on their work permit application? considering that the applicant has applied for the visitor record, after the work permit extension application.
Looking forward to your valuable response.
Sincerely,
threads.answer:
May-25
Good Day,
If the client has maintained (i.e., implied) status, it means that they applied for their Work Permit Extension (WP-EXT) before their current work permit expired and stayed in Canada until they got a decision on this WP-EXT application. When a client has maintained status, they may continue to work under the same conditions as their original permit until we make a decision on their extension application.
If a client fails to submit an extension, or change of permit application, before their current permit expires – they lose their status. If a client wants to stay in Canada and start working again, they must apply to restore their status and get a new work permit. The "restoration period” that you are referring to is the 90-day period after losing status that a client has in order to retore their status. As mentioned, this “restoration period" kicks-in in cases where the client has lost their status. In your case, the client has not lost their status since they are on “maintained status" which is a valid status in Canada. Applying for Visitor Record while the client is on maintained status is allowed. However, if the Visitor Record is approved before the WP-EXT (and while the client is one maintained status) the client's status will change from “maintained status" to "Visitor status”. A Visitor Record is not a work permit, thus the client must stop working. The client cannot resume working until they get a positive decision on their WP-EXT application.
For more information, please consult: I applied for a new work permit. Can I stay in Canada if my work permit expires? Restore your status and get a work permit Temporary residents: Maintained status during processing (previously called implied status)
Thank you kindly, The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

Dear Sir or Madam,
I am seeking clarification regarding how a worker's professional experience is assessed in the context of an immigration
application, when the individual is employed by a Canadian employer.
If an employer fails to comply with their legal obligations — for example, by paying less than the legal minimum wage, failing to declare the employee to tax or social authorities, or not providing legally required paid vacation — can such non-compliance negatively affect the worker's immigration file, even if the individual has genuinely performed the work in question?
In other words, can the fact that the experience was obtained under conditions where the employer was not in compliance with applicable laws lead to the experience being disregarded in an application for permanent residence, a work permit, or another immigration process?

threads.answer:
Inmigration Representatives / Représentants inmigration (IRCC)
Attachments:
~WRD0236.jpg;
Good Day,
Thank you for your question.
IRCC assesses work experience based primarily on whether the applicant genuinely performed the duties of the occupation as described in the National Occupation Classification (NOC), and whether the experience was gained lawfully under the applicable work authorization.
While employer non-compliance with labour laws (e.g., underpayment, failure to remit taxes, or not providing statutory benefits) may be relevant to other agencies (e.g., CRA, ESDC, or provincial labour authorities), the worker's immigration application is not typically penalized solely due to the employer's non-compliance, provided that:
- * The applicant genuinely performed the NOC duties;
- * The work was authorized (i.e., performed under a valid work permit or under a provision of IRPR that authorizes work);
- * The applicant can substantiate the experience with credible documentation (e.g., reference letters, contracts, pay stubs, etc.).
That said, if the employment conditions cast doubt on the genuineness of the claimed work experience, or if there are indications of misrepresentation (e.g., falsified documents or inflated roles), this may negatively affect the application.
To report an employer's non-compliance with the Temporary Foreign Worker Program (TWFP) or International Mobility Program (IMP), you can contact the Employer Contact Centre at 1-800-367-5693.
For more information see this : How to get help.
Thank you kindly,

*** QUESTION 1: The student is typically changing work conditions on an existing study permit, and this doesn't mean applying for a new study permit but fulfilling the off-campus working eligibility. Is this correct? If this is the case, will the student need a PAL to change work conditions on the existing study permit?
RESPoNSE: A student currently in Canada may apply to change the conditions on their existing study permit using the Application to Change Conditions, Extend my Stay or Remain in Canada as a Student [iMM 5709] (the same application used for all in-Canada study permit extension applications).
All study permit applications must include a valid PAL/TAL unless the applicant meets one of the exceptions, which includes applicants who have entered Canada and are applying for a study permit extension at the same Designated Learning Institution (DLI) and the same level of study as their current study permit.
A student who submits a study permit extension application only for the purpose of amending their conditions related to off-campus work eligibility would meet this exception from the PAL/TAL requirement if they remain at the same DLl and level of study.
QUESTION 2: This undergraduate program is not listed under the eligible program CIP codes after the new rules. If the student changes working conditions on the existing study permit after November 1, 2024, is the student considered as changed to a different program of study? As mentioned earlier, the student was admitted to the Pathway to the Undergraduate program in Fall 2024. If on the original LoA, it stated the Upgrading English plus conditional accepted for undergraduate program. Will this be considered as one program, as a pathway is a condition to undergraduate level study? Technically, the student was admitted to study in this undergraduate program and got admitted into it before November 1, 2024, new rules came into effect. If the student applies for a change of work condition on the existing study permit, will this make her ineligible for future PGWP?
RESPONSE: The field of study requirement is based on when the date of receipt of their study permit application. If a student is applying to extend (or change the conditions of) their study permit on or after November 1, 2024, to complete the same program of study for which they had study authorization via the study permit they applied for before November 1, 2024, then the program does not need to meet the field of study requirement to be considered a PGWP-eligible program. In other words, the student's previous study permit (which they applied for before November 1, 2024) must have authorized them to study in the same program as the program specified in the extension application for the program to still be considered PGWP-eligible. If the student applies for a study permit extension on or after November 1, 2024, to start a different program of study, this program must meet the field of study requirement to be considered PGWP-eligible.
For more information, please see the publicly available instruction for officers: Post-graduation work permit (PGWP) [R205(c)

If a statutory holiday falls within an existing scheduled break (with 7 consecutive days), the rules for working unlimited hours would apply. For instance, a holiday on a Monday followed by a 4 day academic break from a Tuesday to a Friday would result in a 7 day academic break. The students have been accepted and intend to study in another program at the same DLl in the same level. Could you please confirm if the student is able to use the same study permit to study in the new program at the same DLí if:
1. 1. The student had already activated their study permit and is currently in Canada RESPONSE: Students who are already in Canada and hold a valid study permit do not need to apply for a new study permit if they are changing their program at the same DLl, provided they are not limited from doing so by conditions imposed on their study permit.
2. 2. The student has received a LOl but has not yet entered Canada and activated their study permit RESPONSE: If a student changes their study program within the same DLl after receiving their LOI but before traveling to Canada, then this change would not affect their previously approved study permit application. If they attend the same DLI, they do not need to reapply for a study permit. When traveling to Canada, they must bring the original and updated Letter of Acceptance from the same DLI along with the original POE letter issued by IRCC, and other required documents to present to CBSA officers. Students in this situation do not need to notify IRCC. If a student changes their program of study to a different DLl after their LOl is issued, they will have to submit a new study permit application to IRCC. Students should immediately submit their new LOA to IRCC using the online web form if they made any changes to their program of study within the same DLl or to a different DLI while their study permit application is still in process.

Minor children who want to study in Canada must apply for a study permit before they enter Canada. This includes minor children who come with parents who already have a valid study or work permit.
Minors coming to Canada with parents who have a valid study or work permit application that has been approved in writing before they come to Canada do not need to provide a letter of acceptance from a designated learning institution (DLI) when applying for a study permit.
Unless they meet one of the exceptions, they must submit a provincial/territorial attestation letter (PAL/TAL) with their application. For example, if they are applying to study at a preschool, primary or secondary school they do not require a PAL/TAL.
