threads.question:
mmigration, Réfugiés
Dear ImmRep,
IRCC has recently added an Education Occupation Category for Express Entry that includes 5 educational occupations.
Most of these Educational occupations work during the school year and are off for 1-2 weeks at Christmas, 1 week at March break, and 11 weeks during the summer. As IRCC deems full-time work to be a minimum of 30 hours per week, my question is how does IRCC calculate full-time work for teachers? Can teachers count regularly scheduled academic breaks towards their period of full-time employment if they returned to work at the end of that period? Or would a teacher have to work for 16-17 consecutive months before they could count themselves as having 1 year of work experience?
Some teachers are contracted for the full year, but are paid over a 10 month period. Some teachers are contracted for the full-year and are paid over 12 months.
In Ontario, teachers only paid for the 194 days of school each year (including non-instructional PA days). For full time tenured teachers, they are paid five-sixths of their salary each pay day (typically once every two weeks), with the remaining one-sixth withheld over the course of the 10 months of the school year. The remaining one-sixth is paid out as a lump sum during the end of the school year (this represents the “summer pay’). Long term occasional teachers (teachers who are on short-term contracts lasting between 11 consecutive school days to 1 school year) are paid their entire salary throughout the year. No salary is withheld and consequently, there is no lump sum pay at the end of the contract.
Each school or school board's collective agreement deems the daily hours of work for a full day assignment for El purposes. For example, the Ottawa Carleton District School Board deems a full-day as 8 hours of work. Teachers cannot generally receive El during their non-teaching periods as they are still considered to be employed [https://www.canada.ca/en/services/benefits/ei/ei-teachers.html](https://www.canada.ca/en/services/benefits/ei/ei-teachers.html)

For example, if a student withdraws and would like to wait to leave Canada while a refund of tuition for the future terms is processed (less than 90 days), must they take action to maintain their status in Canada (i.e. apply for visitor status before they withdraw), or, given the 90-day restoration period, can they remain in Canada without taking action for a maximum of 90 days?

*** The temporary measures to support foreign nationals in response to the crisis in Lebanon are only available to Lebanese nationals and their family members who are already in Canada on a temporary basis and can't return home at this time.
To be eligible for facilitation under the temporary measures to support people affected by the crisis in Lebanon, clients must be:
- * Lebanese nationals in Canada with valid temporary resident status
* foreign national family members of a Canadian citizen or permanent resident who 0* left Lebanon on or after September 29, 2024, and o * are in Canada with valid temporary resident status
* foreign nationals who are affected by the first-generation limit on citizenship as well as their foreign national family members who o* left Lebanon on or after September 29, 2024, and o * are in Canada with valid temporary resident status
- * people who left Lebanon with the help of the Government of Canada on or after September 29, 2024
A client must hold Lebanese citizenship to be considered a Lebanese national and thus be eligible for these temporary measures. A non-Lebanese client may be eligible for these measures if they meet any other eligibility requirement set out above.
For example, clients may be eligible if they arrive as foreign nationals (holding a nationality other than Lebanese) who are family members of Canadian citizens or permanent residents of Canada who fled Lebanon on or after September 29, 2024, due to the deteriorating security situation in the region. As per the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), a foreign national means a person who is not a Canadian citizen or a permanent resident, and includes a stateless person.
Please note that similar temporary measures are available for Palestinian passport holders and their family members. For more information, please visit: Crisis in Lebanon-Canada.ca or Crisis in Israel, the West Bank and the Gaza Strip-Canada.ca.
Please note that the entry requirements are not waived under the above mentioned public policies. Holders of a foreign national passports from visa-required countries and stateless individuals need a visa to come to Canada, for which all standard eligibility and admissibility requirements would apply.

*** In order to be eligible under the temporary special measures, applicants must have been approved under the CUAET measures, arrived in Canada on or before March 31, 2024, and hold valid temporary resident status.
As of August 1, 2024, a temporary public policy was introduced to support certain Ukrainian nationals and their family members who were approved under the CUAET program with insufficient time to arrive in Canada by March 31, 2024. This policy allowed those individuals who were approved for a CUAET temporary resident visa or temporary resident permit on or after February 4, 2024 —referred to as "unprocessed CUAET applicants"—to access limited in-Canada benefits if they arrived by December 31, 2024. However, this facilitative public policy expired on December 31, 2024.
Following the expiry of the above-noted public policy, Ukrainian nationals and their family members who did not arrive in Canada by March 31, 2024, are no longer eligible for CUAET-related facilitation measures, including open work permit extensions.

Response 4: If the student was withdrawn before the legislation changes, it means there was no designated learning institution (DLl) listed on their study permit. As you know, regulation R222(1)(a.1), introduced on November 8, 2024, states that a study permit becomes invalid “on the day the permit holder is no longer enrolled at the designated learning institution named in the permit, other than as a result of completing their studies." Since the student was withdrawn from your institution on October 1, 2024, they were required to take appropriate action at that time—either transfer to a new DLI with plans to study there in Winter 2025, change their status, or leave Canada. Regardless of the study permit's validity date (such as August 31, 2027, in this case), a study permit holder must remain actively enrolled and studying at all times, except during official school breaks.
Response 5: Because the student has completed their last course of the program, it could be deemed that they have completed their studies even though they need to successfully pass that supplemental exam to graduate. R222 1(a) states that a study permit becomes invalid upon the first to occur of the following days: (a) the day that is 90 days after the day on which the permit holder completes their studies.". Normally, their study permit expiry date would coincide with their program length + 90 days.

An eTA is for air travel only. The cancellation or expiration of an eTA does not affect the validity of an individual's work permit or their temporary resident status while in Canada. The eTA is the travel document that the foreign national uses to travel to Canada, whereas a work permit is the status document that grants the foreign national temporary residence status in Canada. Therefore, if an individual is already in Canada with a valid work permit, the expiry of their eTA does not affect their status. They remain authorized to work in Canada until the expiry of their work permit. However, if they leave Canada and plan to return, they require a valid eTA or TRV depending on entry requirements and their mode of transportation. threads.question:
From Dear Sir/Madam,
I am writing for clarification on the following regarding the Home Support Worker Pilot (2021)
- * A client submitted their application under the Home Support Worker Pilot in June 2021 under the Gaining Experience category. In September. she was issued an occupation-specific work permit under the program. The work permit was issued for 24-months, and not the full 36-month duration, due to the expiry of her passport. Her accompanying family members' status documents were issued for the full 36-months. The client was required to return to her home country temporarily due to and her work permit expired while she was outside of Canada. Can she apply from outside of Canada for a new occupation-specific work permit under the program for the remaining 12-months (total of 36-months)?
- * The client had also acquired Canadian work experience required toward her application for permanent residence, but was not able to acquire the full 6-months required before needing to return to her home country. As work experience from both inside and outside of Canada is now accepted in support of the application for permanent residence, can she update the application for permanent residence from outside of Canada with a combination of her Canadian and foreign work experience?
We thank you in advance for your clarification.
and Cizenship Caneda
threads.answer:
Good day, Thank you for contacting the Immigration Represe ntatives Mailbox. Please note that this mailbox is intended for general guidance and does not provide responses to case-specific inquiries but have provided the following information as guidance. Ifyou have case specific questions about a file, you are encouraged to submit the IRCC Web form.
Please see our response to your question.
*** Under the Gaining Experience Category of the Home Support Worker Pilot, the work experience requirement was reduced from 12 months to 6 months effective June 16th 2024. Work experience from inside or outside Canada is accepted. Work experience gained up to 36 months before the application for permanent residence was made will be accepted. In addition, any work experience, Canadian or foreign, gained from the issuance of your occupation restricted work permit up until 36 months from that date will be accepted, as long as the proof is received by IRCC within those 3 years.
If the initial Occupation Restricted Open Work Permit (OROWP) was issued for less than 3 years to align with the passport validity, an extension may be issued for the remaining eligibility period. However, that period must not exceed 3 years from the date the initial work permit was issued under the pilots. As the applicant's OROWP was issued in September of 2023, they may be eligible to have their work permit extended until September 2026.
When an applicant is applying to renew their authorization to work, they are also applying to extend their temporary resident status in Canada. Therefore the applicant would be required to be physically present in Canada at the time they are applying in order to be eligible for the work permit extension. As the applicant is outside of Canada, they may apply for a work permit made outside of Canada and provide a letter of explanation about the situation and why they require the new work permit.
If the applicant already has 6 months of eligible Canadian or foreign experience in the Home support workers, caregivers and related occupations NOC -44101 they can submit their proof of work experience to IRCC along with a completed Schedule 19b as per the instructions on our website. The 6 months of work experience does not have to be continuous to qualify as long as it's within the timeframes mentioned above.
Note that there is nothing preventing an applicant from seeking both an extension of their OROWP and providing their proof of experience to finalize their permanent resident application. However, remember that proof of experience can only be submitted once; if an officer is not satisfied that it's eligible, the permanent residence application may be refused. Applicants should review their documents carefully before sending them.
We trust that this information will assist you.
Thank you kindly,

Please see our response to your question. *** Question 1: Is there any program requirement that effectively requires that the within-Canada Applicant remain in an eligible occupation until their application is accepted, or until another threshold point in the application process?
Response: An applicant is not required to remain employed in the same occupation once they have accumulated the necessary qualifying work experience. However, if they leave the employer who provided the job offer, this may raise concerns about the genuineness of the offer. In addition, applicants in Canada must continue working under the conditions of their current permit or apply for a new work permit if they wish to change employers.
In-Canada applicants who opt to fulfill the job offer requirement instead of the educational requirement, as well as all applicants residing outside Canada, must have a genuine job offer both at the time of their permanent residence (PR) application and at the issuance of their PR visa.
Question 2: Is the option to meet either the educational or job offer requirement “locked-in” at the time of application? The underlying question is whether an Applicant who took advantage of this option must continue to abide by the requirement (in particular, to remain in Canada), or if their eligibility is secure if they were to exit Canada during processing of the PR application.
Response: Education and job offer requirements are determined at the time of application. Additionally, applicants who opted to either meet the job offer or educational requirement must have been in Canada on temporary resident status at time of application. There is no requirement to stay in Canada during application
processing. However, if they are in Canada, they must maintain temporary resident status.
Question 3: If the Applicant seeks an Open Work Permit for Vulnerable Workers (R 207.1), and then begins work in an occupation that is ineligible under the Agri-Food Pilot, does this create any risk of ineligibility or impediment to the underlying PR application? It is understood that work experience gained while on such a permit is acceptable work experience (a policy which we are very thankful for). application, including the necessary work experience. In the three years preceding their application for
permanent residence, they must have accumulated at least 12 months of eligible work experience in Canada. This experience must be in a recognized NOC and NAICS category and obtained while holding a valid work permit. Eligible permits include those issued under the Temporary Foreign Worker Program (supported by a

Bonjour, Merci d’avoir contacté la boîte aux courriels pour les représentants en immigration. Veuillez noter que cette boîte aux lettres est destinée à fournir des conseils généraux et ne fournit pas de réponses à des demandes spécifiques à un cas, mais a fourni les informations suivantes comme conseil. Si vous avez des questions spécifiques à un dossier, nous vous encourageons à soumettre le formulaire Formulaire Web d'IRCC-Canada.ca Veuillez consulter notre réponse à votre question. ***
QUESTION#1:
Employé 1 dans le cadre de l'accord de libre-échange entre le Canada et la Colombie L'employeur a prolongé l’offre d’emploi de son employé au moyen de l’Accord de libre-échange entre le Canada-Colombie et après avoir reçu le nouveau permis de travail, l’employeur a déménagé à une autre ville, mais dans la même région économique de Montréal (il était à Laval et maintenant il est à Sainte-Catherine). Il ne savait pas que cela été considéré un changement des conditions de l'emploi et même si selon EDSC cela est considéré un changement mineur à être signalé, je lui ai recommandé de faire la divulgation volontaire auprès de vous (voir image ci-dessous du site web d'EDSČ).
Alors, vu que ce changement est mineur selon EDSC, je voudrais confirmer avec vous si (voici les questions) :
- Est-ce que l’employé doit demander un nouveau permis de travail pour changer la ville qui est méntionné dans le permis de travail même si cette nouvelle ville fait partie de la même région économique (Changer de Laval à Sainte-Catherine)? Car dans le site web d'IRCC, il parle du lieu de travail relié aux examens médicaux et concernant la section de permis de travail lié à un employeur donné, il ne mentionne pas le lieu de l’emploi (voir image ci-dessous). Si la réponse à la question précédente est oui, est-ce que l'employé doit arrêter de travailler jusqu'à recevoir le nouveau permis de travail ou il pourra continuer à travailler en attendant le nouveau permis de travail vu que le seul changement à faire est la ville, mais le reste de conditions sont les mêmes (employeur, tâches, poste, salaire, etc)?
RÉPONSE :
Un travailleur temporaire peut présenter une demande de prolongation de permis de travail ou de modification de ses conditions de séjour avant sa date d'expiration. Dans ce cas, le demandeur maintient son statut et peut légalement rester au Canada pendant le traitement de leur demande de permis de travail.
Le demandeur de prorogation du permis de travail peut continuer de travailler selon les mêmes conditions que le permis de travail actuel. Cela signifie que si le permis de travail est lié à un employeur donné, il faudrait conserver le même employeur, emploi et lieu de travail.
Dans le cadre du Programme de mobilité internationale (PMl), s'il y a un changement des conditions de travail, incluant le changement du lieu de travail d’une ville à une autre, le client maintient son statut de résident temporaire mais ne peut
nmigration, Réfugiés Cioyenneté Canada pas travailler jusqu'à ce que la demande de prorogation du permis de travail soit traitée. Pour savoir si le demandeur doit cesser de travailler, cela dépend du lieu qui est indiqué sur le permis de travail. Si c'est inscrit, que le lieu de travail est Laval et le nouveau lieu est Sainte-Catherine, alors le client doit obtenir un nouveau permis de travail.
Le client pourrait soumettre une demande pour un nouveau permis de travail et bénéficier de la politique d'intérêt public visant à dispenser les étrangers se trouvant au Canada de certaines exigences quand ils changent d'emploi pour recevoir une autorisation de travail intérimaire jusqu' à ce qu'une décision soit prise sur sa nouvelle demande de permis de travail. Les objectifs de cette politique d’intérêt public consistent à permettrè aux travailleurs étrangers temporaires qui se trouvent déjà au Canada et qui changent d’emploi ou d’employeur, et qui ont obtenu une offre d’emploi au titre du Programme des travailleurs étrangers temporaires ou du Programme de mobilité internationale de commiencer à travailler plus rapidement dans l’attente d’une décision définitive à l'égard de la demande de permis de travail.
Pour faire la demande de changement d'emploi au moyen de la politique d'intérêt de changement d'employeur, veuillez visiter le site web suivant: Prolongation de votre permis ou modification de ses conditions de séjour : Changer d’emploi ou d'employeur-Canada.ca
QUESTION#2 :
Employé 2 dans le cadre de l’accord de libre-échange entre le Canada et la Colombie, mais son permis de travail précédent était basé sur un EIMT L'employé avait un permis de travail fermé basé sur ElMT jusqu’au 31 mars 2025. L’employeur a offert une promotion à son employé avec un offre d’emploi au moyen de l'Accord de libre-échange entre le Canada-Colombie de manière qu'un nouveau permis de travail a été demandé avec la nouvelle adresse de l’employeur avant l’expiration du permis de travail basé sur ElMT ce qui fait que l’employé est sous un statut conservé.
Cependant, vu que l’employeur a déménagé à une autre ville, mais dans la même région économique de Montréal (il était à Laval et maintenant il est à Sainte-Catherine) et Il ne savait pas que cela été considéré un changement des conditions de l’emploi et même si selon EDSC cela est considéré un changement mineur à être signalé, je lui ai recommandé de faire la divulgation volontaire auprès de vous (voir image ci-dessous du site web d’EDSĆ).
Alors, vu que ce changement est mineur selon EDSC et que ceci sera divulgué par l’employeur à EDSC, je voudrais confirmer avec vous si (voici les questions) :
- * Est-ce que l’employé peut continuer de travailler dans l’ancien poste basé sur EIMT (EIMT déjà expiré en même temps que le permis de travail) pendant le statut conservé jusqu'à recevoir le nouveau permis de travail exempté d'ElMT (PT sous ALÉ Canada-Colombie) ou il doit arrêter de travailler jusqu'à recevoir le nouveau permis de travail vu que le seul changement à faire est la ville, mais le reste de conditions sont les mêmes (employeur, tâches, poste, salaire, etc)?
RÉPONSE :
Puisque l'employé 2 a déjà un permis de travail (avec un ElMT) lié à un employeur et il a soumis une demande pour un autre type de permis de travail (au moyen de l'accord de libre-échange Canada Colombie (ALÉCCO), programme de mobilité internationale) il est possible qu'il n’ait pas besoin d'attendre que la demande de permis soit approuvée pour commencer le nouvel emploi. L'employé 2 pourrait bénéficier de la politique d'intérêt public et demander une autorisation de travail intérimaire dans le cadre de cette politique pour changer d'emploi ou d'employeur. Cette politique public l'autoriserait de commencer à travailler pendant que la nouvelle demande de permis de travail est en traitement.
Pour plus d'informations, veuillez consulter les liens suivants: Prolongation de votre permis ou modification de ses conditions de séjour : Que faire si votre permis a expiré-Canada.ca

threads.subject: Temporary Measure: A112025: I am requesting an A11 examination and the issuance of my work permit from within Canada-Do applicants need physical work permit to start working? - REP-B-2025-0597 - Due 3-Jun-25
threads.question:
Subject: Re: FW: Temporary Measure: A : I am requesting an A11 examination and the issuance of my work permit from within Canada-Do applicants need physical work permit to start working? - REP-B-2025-0597 - Due 3-Jun-25
Dear Sirs/Mesdames,
L'nmndmion I am writing to seek clarification regarding the requirement for International Experience Canada (IEC) participants to wait for their physical work permit to arrive in the mail before they are authorized to begin working, even after submitting the A11
Temporary Measure Webform.
I have also noticed recent updates on the IRCC website advising lEC participants that they cannot work until they have received their physical work permit. This appears to contradict the standard procedure for applicants issued work permits inside Canada. Specifically, the guidance states:
"If your work permit will expire before you get your new work permit in the mail, you must apply for a visitor record before your current work permit expires. You can only start working again once you get your new lEC work permit."
While I understand that IEC applications are initially submitted overseas, it is difficult to understand why participants who are already in Canada and contributing to the Canadian economy must stop working after IRCC has issued their new work permit in the system.
Moreover, it is concerning that applicants whose current work permit expires while waiting for their new permit are required to completely cease working, despite the fact that the new work permit has already been issued and is visible in their IRCC secure account. This situation places a significant burden on participants and their employers, especially as they await delivery through regular mail services.
Given the upcoming (and potentially lengthy) Canada Post strike, could IRCC consider allowing lEC participants to resume working once the work permit issuance is confirmed in their IRCC secure account, without having to wait for the mailed document?
For reference, non-IEC applicants are advised:
"We'll send you a note in your online account letting you know your work permit has been approved. You can start working as soon as you receive this note. You don't have to wait until you get your work permit in the mail to start working."
IEC participants and their employers are understandably anxious about the impact postal disruptions may have on maintaining employment and business operations.
Thank you for your attention to this matter. I look forward to your clarification.

IEC participants who have been approved for a work permit will receive a port of entry letter of introduction which they need to submit to a border services officer upon entry to Canada to obtain their work permit. All IEC work permit applications are submitted overseas, and as such their physical work permit will not be mailed to them, unless the lEC participant extending their participation changing their work permit, which is limited to specific situations. In these cases, if there is a change to their lEC work permit, a physical work permit will be mailed to the Canadian address on file. In limited circumstances, a foreign worker can start working before their physical work permit is sent to them. Information on who is eligible to start working before receiving their physical work permit can be found here.

If RTD is considered authorized leave by IRCC, we assume the following PDI section applies: [https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-) manuals/temporary-residents/study-permits/assessing-conditions.html#leave
D. Leave from studies Students may be required or may wish to take leave from their studies while in Canada. For the purpose of assessing if a student is actively pursuing their studies, any leave taken from a program of studies in Canada
should not exceed 150 days from the date the leave commenced and must be authorized by their DLI.
A student on leave who begins or resumes their studies within 150 days from the date the leave commenced (that is, the date the leave was granted by the institution) is considered to be actively pursuing studies during their leave. If a student does not resume their studies within 150 days, they should do either of the following: •* change their status (that is, change to visitor status or worker status)
- * leave Canada
If they do not change their status or leave Canada, they are considered non-compliant with their study permit conditions. In cases where a student has taken multiple periods of leave in Canada during their program of study, the officer should consider the student's reasons for the various periods of leave. If the multiple periods of leave do not appear to support the expectation that the student is making reasonable progress toward the completion of their course or program of study in the time allotted by the course or program of study, the officer may determine that the study permit holder has not fulfilled the condition to actively pursue their course or program of study.
Examples of reasons for leave include but are not limited to the following:
* medical illness or injury
* pregnancy
* family emergency
- * death or serious illness of a family member
- * change in program of study within the same institution, outside a regularly scheduled break
- * dismissals or suspensions (dependent on degree of severity)
- * postponed program start date (see Deferred enrolment for more information)
I would like to confirm impact on legal status for students while on RTD. The recent updates of R222(1) and (a.1), stated study permit becomes invalid 90 days after the permit holder completes their studies or the day on which the permit holder is no longer enrolled at the DLl that is named in the permit.
Since a student on RTD status cannot be enrolled with us during an RTD period, does this mean their study permit becomes invalid the day they are notified of withdrawal from their program? Or will the authorized leave will provide them a status of up to 150 days. Meaning they are not required change their status (that is, change to visitor status or worker status) or leave Canada if they will resume studies at our DLi within 150 days.
Answer
Students may, in exceptional circumstances, may take a leave from their studies. The student must resume classes within 150 days of the date on which they stopped studying. There are various examples of reasons listed on the IRCC website include illness or injury, pregnancy, family emergency, death or serious illness of a family member etc. As of November 8, 2024, IRCC compliance reports are mandatory where the DLI must select the appropriate student's academic status at the DLI. IRCC's website provides several enrollment status options such as leave of absence, deferred enrollment, academic suspension, no longer registered etc. We ask you that you carefully review each definition.
You may find additional information about students who are required to discontinue or a “ required to withdraw” on the IRCC website:
Citoyenneté Canada
1)Academic suspension The student is suspended from your institution, due to poor academic performance or violation of the institution's policies. The student is allowed to return after the period of suspension. Any leave from a program of studies in Canada should not exceed 150 consecutive days from the date the leave started. If a student exceeds 150 days of leave from studies, they will need to change their status with IRCC or will be considered non-compliant with their study permit conditions. Please note that an academic suspension is different than being no longer registered.
2)No longer registered or enrolled Your institution sent the student a letter of admission, but they are no longer registered or enrolled because they have
- * been dismissed
- * withdrawn voluntarily
- * transferred to another institution This status should not be used for students who are academically suspended.
- * 222 (1) A study permit becomes invalid upon the first to occur of the following days:
- * (a.1) the day on which the permit holder is no longer enrolled at the designated learning institution that is named in the permit, other than as a result of completing their studies;

Starting April 2024, IRCC no longer requires language testing for any Provincial Nominee Program (PNP) non-Express Entry application. The PDI updates in April 2024 Language requirements -Provincial nominees-Canada.ca clarified that PNP non-Express Entry clients are no longer required to provide proof of language test results. However, for PNP Express Entry applications, clients still need to provide proof of language proficiency when they apply through the Express Entry system.
Before these changes came into effect, only PNP non-EE, TEER 4 and TEER 5 NOC occupations required language test results to be included in their application. Following the changes, the provinces and territories are responsible to ensure that clients have the language proficiency needed to perform their work duties in one or both of Canada's official languages (French
Question 2: How is the similar situation assessed in the application for Temporary Residence such as Work Permit or/and
While employers may request proof of language proficiency as part of the job offer, most IRCC work permits themselves do not require proof of language proficiency as part of the application. If during the course of application processing an officer determines that they require proof of language proficiency, they will make a case-specific request to the client at that time.
That said, an exception to this is the Post-Graduation Work Permit (PGWP). For PGWP applications submitted on or after November 1, 2024, applicants must demonstrate that they meet the minimum language proficiency requirements in English or French based on their program of study. Language test results must be from an RCC-approved test and must not be less than 2 years old when the PGWP application is received. For more details on language requirements for PGWP applicants, see: Work in Canada after you graduate: Who can apply-Canada.ca. Another work permit program with language
requirements is the Francophone Mobility Work Permit which requires that the client be able to prove their speaking and listening skills in French are at an intermediate level (NCLC Level 5 or higher). Please consult the Francophone Mobility work permit: How to apply webpage for information on what types of documents can be submitted to prove French language proficiency. While most work permits do not require proof of language proficiency, clients are encouraged to read through the eligibility requirements for their respective work permit stream to see if they will need to prove language proficiency, or provide a language test upfront.
For Study Permits:
Study permit applicants under the Francophone Minority Communities student pilot (FMCSP) must be able to prove that their French speaking, listening, reading and writing skills are at a level 5 or higher in the Niveaux de compétence linguistique canadiens scale. Test results submitted with the application must not be dated more than 2 years from the date of issuance.

Foreign nationals who wish to immigrate to Canada are required to apply for and obtain a permanent resident visa from outside of the country. Foreign nationals do not have the right to apply for permanent residence from within Canada unless they fulfill the requirements of an in-Canada immigration class.
However, section A25(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA) allows foreign nationals who are inadmissible or who are ineligible to apply in an immigration class, to apply for permanent residence, or for an exemption

for H&C consideration is an exceptional measure-it is not simply another means of applying for permanent resident status in Canada.

The following persons, whether they have left Canada voluntarily or not, require the written authorization of an officer in order to return to Canada:
- all persons issued a deportation order and removed from Canada (R226);

- all persons issued a departure order, who failed to leave Canada within the prescribed 30-day period and have consequently been deemed deported from Canada (R224(2)).

Bonjour,
Merci d’avoir contacté la boîte aux courriels pour les représentants en immigration.
Veuillez noter que cette boîte aux lettres est destinée à fournir des conseils généraux et ne fournit pas de réponses à des demandes spécifiques à un cas, mais a fourni les informations suivantes comme conseil. Si vous avez des questions spécifiques à un dossier, nous vous encourageons à soumettre le formulaire Formulaire Web d'IRCC-Canada.ca Veuillez consulter notre réponse à votre question.
Il n'y a aucune obligation pour une personne protégée de demander la résidence permanente. C'est à elle de choisir.
Les personnes protégées peuvent continuer à résider au Canada et sont protégées contre le refoulement par l'article 115(1) de la loi sur l'immigration et la protection des réfugiés.
115 (1) Ne peut être renvoyée dans un pays où elle risque la persécution du fait de sa race, de sa religion, de sa nationalité, de son appartenance à un groupe social ou de ses opinions politiques, la torture ou des traitements ou peines cruels et inusités, la personne protégée ou la personne dont il est statué que la qualité de réfugié lui a été reconnue par un autre pays vers lequel elle peut être renvoyée. Cependant, il est important de prendre en compte les avantages de la résidence permanente. Par exemple, à moins qu'elle ne devienne un résident permanent, une personne protégée continuera à avoir besoin d'un permis de travail et, si elle n'est plus mineure, d'un permis d'études si elle souhaite travailler ou étudier au Canada. En outre, si la personne protégée souhaite que les membres de sa famille vivant à l'étranger la rejoignent au Canada en tant que résidents permanents, elle
doit d'abord devenir elle-même un résident permanent.
La personne protégée doit également vérifier auprès de sa province ou de son territoire de résidence s'il existe une
différence d'éligibilité aux services entre les personnes protégées et les résidents permanents.

RESPONSE: Aforeign national may not perform work in Canada unless authorized, as per section 196 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR). If a student holds an employer-specific work permit, they must adhere to the conditions of the permit, including only working for that specific employer. If they would like to work for a different employer, they must obtain authorization to do so (e.g., apply for a co-op work permit).
The student must have a valid study permit to be eligible for a co-op work permit – they may apply for a study permit and co-op work permit at the same time.
As per the above, the duration of the study permit should be for the duration of the in-Canada portion only.

threads.subject: Question-fin de l'autorisation de travail pour les étudiants étrangers qui achèvent un programme d'études · REP-B-2025-0937 - Due 8-Jul-25
threads.question:
Bonjour,
Je vous écris afin d’obtenir un éclaircissement de votre part quant aux questions suivantes :
1. 1. Quel est le moment précis auquel les étudiants étrangers n’ayant pas encore présenté une demande de permis d’études ou de travail subséquent ou une demande d’admission à un autre programme d’études doivent cesser de travailler en vertu de l’autorisation conférée par leur permis d'études?
2. 2. Plus spécifiquement, concrètement, à partir de quel moment IRCC considère qu’ils ont satisfait aux dernières exigences de
and Citizenshi Canada et Ciloyeneé Canada
leur programme d’études? Est-ce le moment qui suit immédiatement la tenue du dernier examen ou dernier jour de stage?
3. 3. Plus spécifiquement, concrètement, comment établir qu'ils ont reçu une confirmation écrite de leur EED indiquant la fin du programme d’études? Ou plutôt, comment établir, pour un employeur qui embaucherait ces étudiants, qu’ils n’ont PAS ENCORE REçU telle confirmation, et seraient donc encore en droit de travailler malgré la fin des études?
4. 4. Comment se concilient les dispositions des articles 222(1) particulièrement c) et 220.1(1)b) du Règlement sur l’immigration et la protection des réfugiés avec l’indication suivante « Ils peuvent travailler jusqu'à la date à laquelle ils reçoivent la confirmation écrite de leur établissement d’enseignement indiquant qu’ils ont terminé leur programme d’études (p. ex. courriel, lettre, relevé de notes ou diplôme), pourvu que leur permis d’études demeure valide pendant cette période. » (source : Permis d'études : Travail hors campus-Canada.ca)?
5. 5. Concrètement, à partir du moment où l’étudiant a terminé son programme (tenue du dernier examen ou dernier jour de stage), l’étudiant est-il encore considéré suivre activement son cours, respecter les conditions de son permis d'études, et donc en mesure de se prévaloir de l’autorisation de travail conférée par le permis d’études?
Vous remerciant par avance de vos précisions, je vous souhaite une très agréable fin de journée,
threads.answer:
Bonjour,
Merci d’avoir contacté la boîte aux courriels pour les représentants en immigration. Veuillez noter que cette boîte aux lettres est destinée à fournir des conseils généraux et ne fournit pas de réponses à des demandes spécifiques à un cas, mais a fourni les informations suivantes comme conseil. Si vous avez des questions spécifiques à un dossier, nous vous encourageons à soumettre le formulaire Formulaire Web d'IRCC-Canada.ca Veuillez consulter notre réponse à votre question.
1. 1. Quel est le moment précis auquel les étudiants étrangers n'ayant pas encore présenté une demande de permis d’études ou de travail subséquent ou une demande d’admission à un autre programme d'études doivent cesser de travailler en vertu de l’autorisation conférée par leur permis d'études? Réponse : Les étudiants peuvent travailler hors campus à temps partieldans les cas suivants :
- * ils répondent aux critères d’admissibilité du permis de travail hors campus [R186v)];
- * ils ont satisfait aux dernières exigences de leur programme d’études, mais n’ont pas encore reçu la confirmation écrite de la part de l’établissement indiquant qu’ils ont terminé le programme avec succès (p. ex. relevé de notes, lettre officielle, courriel officiel);
- * ils n’ont pas présenté une demande de permis de travail (p. ex. permis de travail postdiplôme ou permis de travail accompagné d’une étude d’impact sur le marché du travail valide) ou une demande de prorogation du permis d’études, et ne sont pas inscrits à un autre programme d’études.
Ils peuvent travailler jusqu’à la date à laquelle ils reçoivent la confirmation écrite de leur établissement d’enseignement indiquant qu’ils ont terminé leur programme d’études (p. ex. courriel, lettre, relevé de notes ou diplôme), pourvu que leur permis d’études demeure valide pendant cette période. Pour plus d’informations, veuillez
visiter notre site web : Permis d'études : Travail hors campus-Canada.ca.
2. 2. Plus spécifiquement, concrètement, à partir de quel moment IRCC considère qu'ils ont satisfait aux dernières exigences de leur programme d'études? Est-ce le moment qui suit immédiatement la tenue du dernier examen ou dernierjour de stage? Réponse : Dès qu’un étudiant a reçu l’un des documents suivants : lettre officielle de fin d’études; relevé de notes; un courriel de son établissement l’informant qu’il a terminé son programme, ou diplôme, il est considéré avoir complété son programme d’études.
3. 3. Plus spécifiquement, concrètement, comment établir qu'ils ont reçu une confirmation écrite de leur EED indiquant la fin du programme d'études? Ou plutôt, comment établir, pour un employeur qui embaucherait ces étudiants, qu'ils n'ont PAS ENCORE REÇU telle confirmation, et seraient donc encore en droit de travailler malgré la fin des études? Réponse : L’étudiant et son employeur doivent s’assurer que l’étudiant a les autorisations nécessaires pour travailler pendant ses études. S’il est autorisé à travailler pendant ces études, cela sera indiqué dans les conditions figurant sur
Cioyenneté Canada
son permis d'études. En tant que titulaire de permis d’études, l’étudiant doit respecter un certains nombre de conditions en lien avec son autorisation de travail. S’ils ne respectent plus ces conditions, il en est de sa responsabilité d’informer son employeur.
4. 4. Comment se concilient les dispositions des articles 222(1) particulièrement c) et 220.1(1)b) du Règlement sur l'immigration et la protection des réfugiés avec l'indication suivante « /ls peuvent travailler jusqu'à la date à laquelle ils reçoivent la confirmation écrite de leur établissement d'enseignement indiquant qu'ils ont terminé leur programme d’études (p. ex. courriel, lettre, relevé de notes ou diplôme), pourvu que leur permis d’études demeure valide pendant cette période. » (source : Permis d'études : Travail hors campus-Canada.ca)? Réponse : Si le permis d’études devient invalide [au titre de l’article R222] avant que l’étudiant reçoive la confirmation de la part de son établissement d’enseignement indiquant qu’il a terminé son programme d’études, l’étudiant doit cesser de travailler la journée à laquelle son permis d’études devient invalide, à l’exception de s’il a un statut maintenu. Le respect de l’article R220.1(1)b) est évaluée sur plusieurs critères dont l’inscription à un établissement d’enseignement désigné (EED), la réussite des cours, entre autres. Veuillez-vous référez à la page suivante pour plus d'informations : Permis d'études : Évaluation des conditions liées à un permis d'études.
5. 5. Concrètement, à partir du moment où l'étudiant a terminé son programme (tenue du dernier examen ou dernier jour de stage), l’étudiant est-il encore considéré suivre activement son cours, respecter les conditions de son permis d’études, et donc en mesure de se prévaloir de l'autorisation de travail conférée par le permis d'études? Réponse : Voir les réponses aux questions précédentes.
Nous espérons que ces informations vous seront utiles. *** Cordialement,
La boîte aux courriels pour les représentants en immigration

*** As of January 21, 2025, spousal open work permits are limited to the spouses or common-law partners of temporary workers employed in TEER 0 or 1 occupations, or select TEER 2 or 3 occupations. Specifically, this change means that family members, of workers in lower-skilled jobs are no longer eligible for open work permits.
Open work permits issued for family members under previous measures that have not expired will still be valid. In situations where family members received a work permit with a duration that is shorter than the work permit of the principal applicant, in-Canada family members (including spouses and common-law partners as well as dependent children) can apply to renew their work permit as per the requirements of the pre-January 21 measure as long as they are applying under the same criteria as their current work permit, and the requested duration of the renewal matches that of the existing work permit of the principal applicant.
If the principal applicant has since received another work permit, the spouse is subject to the post-January 21 rules, and in this case, they would not be eligible to apply for an extension and will need to submit a new work permit application.
Family members who are no longer entitled to an open work permit can apply for any type of work permit for which they may be eligible under Canada's work permit programs.

Citizenship Act-REP-B-2025-0879 - Due 2-Jul-25
Good day,
Thank you for contacting the Immigration Representatives Mailbox. Please note that this mailbox is intended for general guidance and does not provide responses to case-specific inquiries but have provided the following information as guidance. Ifyou have case specific questions about a file, you are encouraged to submit the IRCC Web form.

*** Being under a peace bond does not prevent a person from obtaining citizenship or taking the oath of citizenship as long as the person is not subject to any other prohibitions set out in section 22 of the Citizenship Act. Section 22 of the Act describes situations that may prohibit a person from obtaining citizenship or taking the oath of citizenship.
Specifically,
* Under paragraph 22(1)(a), no person is, under any law in force in Canada: (i) subject to a probation order, (ii) an inmate on parole, or (iii) serving a sentence of imprisonment. Since a person on a peace bond is not on probation, an inmate on parole or serving a prison sentence, the prohibition in section 22(1)(a) would not apply.
* Under subsection 22(2), a person is prohibited from: being convicted of an offense under the Citizenship Act, or of an indictable offense under any other federal law (i) during the period of four years immediately before the date of the person's application, or (ii) while the request is being processed. Because a peace bond does not result in a conviction, a prohibition under subsection 22(2) would not apply. *** Thank you kindly,

As you are aware, there are two different paragraphs in the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR) where the work of a foreign national transferring from a position in a foreign enterprise to a Canadian enterprise with a qualifying Paragraph R204(a) applies where Canada has an international free trade agreement (FTA) which includes provisions for intra-
company transfers (ICTs). The instructions for processing applications for foreign nationals under trade agreements are found at International Mobility Program: International Free Trade Agreements.
Paragraph R205(a) applies to the IMP category for all foreign nationals, regardless of citizenship, if their transfer will create or
maintain significant social, cultural or economic benefits or opportunities for Canadian citizens or permanent residents.
Canada's commitments under the General Agreement on Trade in Services (GATS) with respect to temporary entry of ICTs are processed under R205(a) and specified under administrative codes C62 and C63. The instructions are found at ntra-company transferees: Canadian interests —International Mobility Program.
To be eligible under either provision of the IRPR, ICT applicants must be currently employed in an executive, managerial, or specialized knowledge capacity by an enterprise of a multinational corporation (MNC) outside of Canada.
As per the operational guidelines for processing ICTs under R205(a), the administrative exemption code for Executives or Managers is C62. When Officers are reviewing the work permit applications under C62, they are instructed to ensure that the occupational code and title are in the appropriate Training, Education, Experience and Responsibilities (TEER) category for the occupation capacity.
In the operational guidelines for C62, Officers are instructed that TEER 0 is for an executive and TEER 1 is for a manager. The manual provides the following definition for each category, again specifying the appropriate TEER for each category:
Executive capacity (TEER 0) means that the employee primarily:
- * directs the management of the enterprise or a major component or function of the enterprise;
- * establishes the goals and policies of the enterprise, component, or function;
- * exercises wide latitude in discretionary decision-making; and
- * receives only general supervision or direction from higher level executives, the board of directors, or stockholders of the enterprise.
Managerial capacity (TEER 1) means that the employee primarily:
- * manages the enterprise, a department, subdivision, a component or an essential function of the enterprise;
- * oversees and controls the work of: o * other managers or supervisors;
o * professional employees; or o * an essential function within the enterprise;
- * has the authority to recommend or to hire, fire or make other personnel decisions, such as promotion and leave authorization. Where they do not directly supervise employees, the manager functions at a senior level within the hierarchy of the enterprise;
- * exercises discretion over the day-to-day operations of the activity or function for which the employee has the authority.
For ICTs pursuant to R204(a), in which the FTA allows for the intra-company transfer of Executives or Managers, the instructions for Officers with respect to assessing the appropriate TEER category for Executives or Managers are slightly different to the above, and state as follows: “Ensure that the occupational code and title are in the appropriate TEER for the occupation capacity. For example: TEER 0 or 1 for an executive". The policy does not state the TEER for a Manager, although the policy then provides the same definition as above for Executive capacity (TEER 0) and Managerial capacity (TEER 1).
Please see the TEER instructions for the Canada-United States-Mexico Agreement (CUSMA) agreement here as an example. The guidance for the other FTAs are identical. The only exception is with respect to the policy under the Canada-Ukraine Free Trade Agreement (CUFTA), which states as follows when assessing the appropriate NOC: Is the occupation a position as an executive; a manager; a specialist. Later in the instructions, the guidance is as follows: “This group includes foreign nationals in the executive or managerial capacity. In the National Occupational Classification this would the Training, Experience, Education and Requirements (TEER) categories of 0 or 1”. See the CUFTA policy here.
Citoyenneté Canada
Question:
In light of the above policy, I am writing to ask for clarification on whether, contrary to the instructions provided above, foreign nationals can apply as an ICT Manager, under both R204(a) and R205(a), in a position that is TEER 0, as opposed to being limited to occupations falling under TEER 1 (assuming they meet the other definition requirements of Managerial Capacity).
This question is particularly important when reviewing the types of occupations that fall under the TEERs. The instruction provided to Officers for processing ICTs under R205(a), and for the large majority of ICTs under R204(a) (minus CUFTA), suggests that the foreign national is required to be in a TEER 0 occupation to qualify as an Executive, or TEER 1 to qualify as a Manager. However, a review of the occupations under TEER 0 in the NOC 2021 Version 1.0 indicate that the large majority (if not all) of managerial capacity positions are TEER 0. TEER 1 positions are better described as occupations usually requiring a university degree. To provide an example, a Civil Engineer is a TEER 1 position (21300), whereas an Engineering Manager is a TEER 0 position (20010). However, as per the instructions, an Engineering Manager would be required to be in a TEER 1 position, rather than TEER 0, to qualify as an ICT Manager.
My thoughts on what could have happened here are that the instructions may have been carried over from the previous NOC 2016 Version 1.3, in which Managerial positions such as Engineering Manager (0211) were Skill Level A – Occupations usually requiring a university education. It could be that the instructions for Skill Level A were applied to TEER 1 - Occupations usually requiring a university education in the updated instructions, without accounting for the fact that TEER 0 is the more appropriate category for individuals qualifying under ICT in a Managerial Capacity.
Can you please clarify? My primary concern is around eligibility for ICT as a Manager in a TEER 0 occupation based on a strict reading of the instructions above. If Managers under TEER 0 occupations are indeed eligible as an ICT Manager, which I assume they are, we would suggest updating the policy to make that clear. To make it easier, we would suggest adopting the language of the instructions as they are already written under CUFTA, here, which allow for Executives or Managers to qualify under either TEER 0 or 1, without the distinction.
Thank you kindly for your consideration.
Kind Regards,

When the person being sponsored for permanent residence applies for an open work permit, they must be

Dear Officer,
This is a follow up to my previous question regarding sponsoring a spouse while receiving RAP benefits. On Sun, Jan 30, 2022 at 12:43 'a0PM wrote:
Good day, Thank you for contacting the Immigration Representatives Mailbox.
Social assistance means any benefit, whether money, goods or services, provided to or on behalf of a person by a province under a program of social assistance. It includes assistance for food, shelter, clothing, fuel, utilities, household supplies, personal requirements and health care not provided by public health care.
RAP does not meet the definition of social assistance. However; this doesn't guarantee the approval of an application. The applicant cannot be in receipt of social assistance throughout the processing of the application. If the applicant receives social assistance after the end of the period of receiving RAP and before the PR application is finalized, doing so may result in not being an eligible sponsor.
You may not be eligible to sponsor your spouse, if you receive social assistance for a reason other than a disability.
You can find more information about eligibility to sponsor your spouse here: [https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-)

Good day,
Thank you for contacting the Immigration Representatives Mailbox.
Please note that this mailbox is intended for general guidance and does not provide responses to case-specific inquiries but have provided the following information as guidance. If you have case specific questions about a file, you are encouraged to submit the IRCC Web form.
Please see our response to your question.
A Canadian PR who is receiving Resettlement Assistance Program (RAP) benefits may sponsor their spouse as long as they are not in receipt of social assistance from the day the application is filed until the day a decision is made with respect to the application and meet all other requirements to sponsor.
The Government of Canada, through the Resettlement Assistance Program (RAP), provides federally administered financial assistance to eligible clients in the form of one-time start-up and monthly income support to help with basic needs of life such as food, incidentals, shelter, and other expenses needed to establish themselves in Canada.
Section 2 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR), defines social assistance as follows:
any benefit in the form of money, goods or services provided to or on behalf of a person by a province under a program of social assistance, including a program of social assistance designated by a province to provide for basic requirements including food, shelter, clothing, fuel, utilities, household supplies, personal requirements and health care not provided by public health care, including dental care and eye care.
What is considered social assistance: Some benefits (money, goods or services) from provinces or territories are considered to be social assistance for the purpose of sponsoring. This includes assistance from the government to cover basic needs like: food shelter clothing fuel utilities household supplies health care not covered by public health care (extra benefits paid by the government to low-income people or others in need)
What isn't considered social assistance: Social assistance doesn't include: •Employment Insurance
and Citizenship Caneda
provincial student loans
immigration loans subsidized housing
tax credits child care subsidies public health care (services your province or territory gives to all people who live there)
other benefits widely available to residents, including people who are working
Provinces and territories had temporary programs to help people cope with the COVID-19 pandemic. We don't consider these benefits to be social assistance if they aren't considered as such by the province or territory.
Also not considered social assistance:
Canada Recovery Caregiving Benefit (now closed)
Canada Recovery Sickness Benefit (now closed) Canada Recovery Benefit (now closed)
Canada Emergency Response Benefit (now closed)
Canada Emergency Student Benefit (now closed)
A sponsorship application can only be approved if a sponsor is not in receipt of social assistance (for a reason other than disability) from the day the application is filed to the day a decision is made. As RAP income support is a federal support (and not provincial or territorial), it is not considered to be social assistance under the IRPR. Therefore, a sponsor who is only in receipt RAP income support would not be barred from sponsoring their spouse under section
133(1)(k) of the IRPR. For more information on who can sponsor, see:

1. 1. IRCC interprets academic suspension as a temporary leave from studies, during which a student is still considered enrolled at the designated learning institution (DLl). If the suspension does not exceed 150 days and the student remains in Canada, their study permit remains valid. To protect their legal status during this interim period, students should apply for a visitor record as a temporary resident. This ensures continuous compliance with IRCC regulations and avoids gaps in status, especially if the appeal outcome is favorable.

Thank you for reaching out. Please see the responses to your questions below.
1. 1. Whether a worker who received a closed work permit after June 7, 2023, is required to obtain a study permit to enroll in a program of six months or less? Eligibility criteria for the public policy pertains to the date that the application was received by IRCC, and not the date that the work permit document was received by the applicant. In order to qualify under this public policy, the work permit or work permit extension application must have been received on or before June 7, 2023. A worker who applied for a work permit after June 7, 2023 is not eligible for the measures outlined in the public policy. A study permit is not required for a foreign national to enroll in a study program of six months of less; however, the foreign national must ensure that they remain in compliance with all conditions and remarks stated on their valid work permit.
2. 2. If the study program exceeds six months, is a study permit mandatory, regardless of the date the work permit was issued? A work permit holder may study without a work permit until the expiry of the work permit or the date that the public policy expires (June 27, 2026) if they meet eligibility criteria under the public policy. If the foreign national does not meet criteria under the public policy and intends to study for more than six months, then they will be required to obtain authorization to study through issuance of a valid study permit prior to commencing their studies. For details regarding the public policy, please visit our website: Public policy allowing some work permit holders to study without a study permit-Canada.ca
3. 3. If the program includes a co-op or internship component, is a separate co-op work permit required? If the Foreign National (FN) is studying without a study permit under this public policy and wants to start a co-op work placement, they may need to apply for a new employer-specific work permit before the co-op placement starts. Open work permit holders don't need to apply for a new work permit. Employer-specific work permit holders The FN only needs a new work permit if their co-op employer or occupation is different from their current employer or occupation. The conditions on their new work permit must match their new co-op employer or occupation. In this case, they'll hold 2 valid work permits at the same time:
1. their original work permit, which authorizes them to study under this public policy
2. a second work permit authorizing them to complete their co-op placement
Please consult the "If you have another type of work permit" dropdown in the Public policy allowing some work permit holders to study without a study permit-Canada.ca webpage for more details, especially other documents the FN may need in order to be eligible.
We trust that this information will assist you.

1. 1. Can someone apply for an inland sponsorship application from within Canada and then leave the country for a few days on vacation, assuming they have legal status to return? A person applying under the spouse or common-law partner in Canada class (SCLPC) may travel outside of Canada (with or without their sponsor) on a temporary basis, such as for a short trip; however they must still satisfy an officer that they are cohabiting with their sponsor in Canada to be considered a member of SCLPC class. The longer the time spent apart and/or outside of Canada, the more difficult it may be to establish that they are cohabiting in Canada with their sponsor; however each case will be assessed individually. An officer may also request additional information if they have concerns that an applicant does not meet certain requirements. As per section 124 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR), A foreign national is a member of the spouse or common-law partner in Canada class if they
a. a. are the spouse or common-law partner of a sponsor and cohabit with that sponsor in Canada;
In general, cohabitation means living together. Two people who are cohabiting have combined their affairs and set up their household together in one dwelling. While cohabitation means living together continuously, from time to time, one or the other spouse may leave the home for work or business travel, family obligations and so on. The separation must be temporary and short.
If leaving Canada, foreign nationals should ensure that they have the proper (and valid) visa or documents required to re-enter Canada. It should also be noted that there is no guarantee that foreign nationals who have left Canada after submitting an application under the Spouse or Common-law Partner in Canada class will be allowed to return to or re-enter Canada. If they are unable to do so, their application for permanent residence may be refused because they are not cohabiting with their spouse or common-law partner at the time the case is finalized [R72(1)(d) and R124(a)].
2. 2. Can someone apply for an outland sponsorship application even if they are physically present in Canada? A person applying as a spouse or common-law partner can apply under the overseas family class even if they are physically present in Canada. For more information about the different classes of application see the Complete Guide. It is up to the applicant to choose
and Cizenship Canedaot Cioyenneté Canada
the class of application that best fits their personal situation.
Applicants applying under the overseas family class who are either currently living in Canada or later come to Canada on temporary resident status must continue to comply with and meet the requirements set out in the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act and Regulations. This includes maintaining temporary resident status in Canada throughout the processing of the permanent resident application.
A foreign national who remains in Canada without valid status/authorization could be found to be inadmissible for non- compliance with the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA) and Regulations due to their lack of status and failure to leave Canada at the end of their authorized stay, and as a result, their PR application under the overseas family class may be refused.

SECTION CONCERNÉE :
Un demandeur conserve son statut de résident temporaire pendant la période de traitement de sa demande de prolongation uniquement s’il a présenté sa demande avant l’expiration de son statut et s’il demeure au Canada.

Si le demandeur présente une demande subséquente afin de prolonger son statut après son expiration, il ne bénéficiera pas du statut conservé pendant la période de traitement de la demande subséquente. Good day,
Thank you for contacting the Immigration Representatives Mailbox. Please note that this mailbox is intended for general guidance and does not provide responses to case-specific inquiries but have provided the following information as guidance. Ifyou have case specific questions about a file, you
are encouraged to submit the IRCC Web form. Please see our response to your question.
*** Thank you for reaching out to us with your question on Monday, June 30, 2025, regarding International Experience Canada and its Recognized Organizations.
Recognized Organizations (ROs) are Canada-based organizations that help youth work and travel internationally through International Experience Canada (IEC). They provide optional fee-based support services to both Canadian and foreign national youth wishing for assistance with their international experience.
Youth interested in IEC are not obligated to use an RO; they can choose to use an RO for more support before or during
their experience. ROs typically provide pre- and post-arrival orientation services; job finding or preparation (e.g.
resume review/support, interview practice/support, job boards/lists); accommodations arrangement or finding
services; and emergency support services. Service options vary between ROs based on the nature of programming, destination country, and type of international experience. ROs may charge fees for their services, which are not recruitment fees, and IRCC monitors fees and fee changes to ensure that they are transparent and reflective of the services provided.
Historically, most foreign national youth coming to Canada on lEC, including those using an RO, participate in the Working Holiday stream, which provides foreign national youth with an open work permit that lets them work for almost any employer in Canada and change jobs or locations throughout their experience.
For the smaller number of lEC youth that participate in the employer-specific streams (Young Professional or International Coop), the job must count toward professional development or be directly linked to their field of study, and the employer must pay the employer compliance fee ($230) and submit a job offer via the Employer Portal. If the caregiving work involves providing personal care services in a residential setting, such as senior communities, the job offer may qualify. Officers will use all available information to determine whether the applicant will be providing services that align with the NOC and whether the work setting is considered the care recipient's private residence rather than an institution.
3. Long-Term Care Homes: Job offers from long-term care homes are not eligible under this category. The program excludes caregiving work performed in institutional settings, such as nursing homes or long-term care homes.

threads.subject: Clarification Regarding Eligibility for Temporary or Permanent Residence Applications – Out of Status Individuals
threads.question:
Dear Sir/Madam, IC member in good standing-CIC( would appreciate your guidance on this important matter, as it is not
clearly outlined in the operational manuals
In a case where an applicant is out of status in a country (outside Canada) and has entered that country illegally, are they still eligible to apply for temporary visas or permanent residence? Additionally, are there any exceptions to this rule when the application is submitted under the Family Class category?
In addition, What if the applicant is out of status in Canada and has entered illegally?
Your clarification would be greatly appreciated.
Kind regards,
threads.answer:
- REP-B-2025-0428 - Due 20-May-25
Good day,
Thank you for contacting the Immigration Representatives Mailbox. Please note that this mailbox is intended for general guidance and does not provide responses to case-specific inquiries but have provided the following information as guidance. Ifyou have case specific questions about a file, you
are encouraged to submit the IRCC Web form.
Please see our response to your question.
*** Apologies for our delay in responding and thank you for contacting the Immigration Representatives Mailbox.
If an applicant is out of status in a country (outside of Canada) and has entered that country illegally, are they still eligible to
apply for permanent residence under the family class category?
A person who is out of status in a country outside of Canada may apply for permanent residence under the family class, provided they meet the eligibility requirements of the class and are not inadmissible for reasons such as security, criminal or medical.
For more information about sponsoring family members and requirements, see Sponsor your family members to immigrate to Canada-Canada.ca
As per Section 16(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), a foreign national must answer truthfully all questions put to them, including their current immigration status in their country of residence.
Depending on their nationality, age, time spent residing in their current country of residence and type of application, the applicant may need to submit a police certificate from their current country of residence. Officers may also request additional
police certificates as necessary.
A foreign national may be considered criminally inadmissible to Canada as per Section 36(1)(c) or Section 36(2)(c) of the IRPA if their illegal entry or presence in their country of residence constitutes a criminal offence under that country's laws and if that offence, if committed in Canada would be considered: o * an indictable offence in Canada (Criminality, A36(2)(c)); or o * an offence punishable in Canada by a maximum term of imprisonment of at least 10 years (Serious Criminality, A36(1)(c)).
Lastly, in order to obtain permanent resident status, a family class applicant must also hold one of the documents listed in section R50(1) of the Regulations such as a passport or travel document [see R50(1) for the complete list].
If an applicant is out of status in Canada or has entered illegally, can they apply for permanent residence under the Family Class?:
There are two main streams of family sponsorship:
- * Overseas family class
- * Spouse and common-law partner in Canada (SCLPC) class
A person may apply under the overseas family class if:
- * They are being sponsored as a spouse or common-law partner and are living outside Canada
- * They are being sponsored as a spouse or common-law partner and are currently living in Canada but do not plan to stay in Canada while the application is being processed
- * Their sponsor plans to appeal if the application is refused
- * They are being sponsored as a conjugal partner, dependent child, parent or grandparent, adopted child/child to be adopted, or other relative.
A person may apply under the SCLPC class if they are being sponsored as a spouse or common-law partner, and they:
- * live with their sponsor in Canada
- * have valid temporary resident status in Canada, or are exempt from needing this status under a public policy
For more information on selecting the category of application see the Complete Guide.
A foreign national who remains in Canada without valid status/authorization could be found to be inadmissible for non- compliance with the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA) and Regulations due to their lack of status and failure to leave Canada at the end of their authorized stay, and as a result, their PR application under the overseas family class may be refused.
Out of status spouses or common-law partners residing in Canada applying under the SCLPC class may be exempt from the requirement to have status in Canada if they meet the requirements of this public policy.
The effect of the policy is to exempt applicants under the SCLPC class from the requirement under Section 124(b) of the Regulations to be in status and the requirements under A21(1) and R72(1)(e)(i) of the IRPA/IRPR to not be inadmissible due to a lack of status; however, all other requirements of the class apply.
For the purposes of this public policy, persons with a “lack of status" refers to those in the following situations:
- * persons who have overstayed a visa, visitor record, work permit, study permit or temporary resident permit
- * persons who have worked or studied without being authorized to do so as prescribed by the Act
- * persons who have entered Canada without a visa or other document required by the Regulations
- * persons who have entered Canada without a valid passport or travel document (provided valid documents are acquired by the time IRCC seeks to grant permanent residence)
- * persons who elude examination upon entry to Canada.
Lack of status does not refer to any other inadmissibilities including:
- * failure to obtain permission to enter Canada after being deported
- * persons who have entered Canada with a fraudulent or improperly obtained passport, travel document or visa and who have used the document for misrepresentation under IRPA.
- * persons under removal orders or facing enforcement proceedings for reasons other than the above-noted lack of status reasons.
The above response provides information only as it relates to family class permanent resident programs. If you require information about other programs, please specify the program or category for which you require additional information.
We hope this information is useful for you.
Thank you kindly,
and Citizenshi Canada et Ciloyeneé Canada

Un personne avec un statut de résident temporaire peut faire du bénévolat à condition que :
l’activité qui ne diminue pas vraiment, pour les Canadiens ou résidents permanents, les occasions d’avoir de l’emploi ou de l’expérience dans le marché du travail ne sont pas considérées comme du « travail » au sens de la définition.
Exemples d’activités pour lesquelles une personne ne recevrait normalement pas de rémunération ou ne serait pas en concurrence directe avec les citoyens canadiens ou les résidents permanents sur le marché du travail canadien et qui seraient normalement accomplies à temps partiel ou liées aux motifs de la présence de la personne au Canada (liste non exhaustive) :
- * travail bénévole pour lequel une personne ne serait pas normalement rémunérée, comme le fait de siéger au conseil d’une institution religieuse ou de bienfaisance; d’être un « grand frère » ou une « grande sœur » d’un enfant, faire de la téléassistance à un centre d’aide aux victimes d’agression sexuelle (normalement cette activité se ferait à temps partiel et ne découle pas de la raison principale de la présence de la personne au Canada);
- * aide non rémunérée d’un ami ou d’un membre de la famille durant une visite, comme une mère qui aide sa fille dans la garde de son enfant ou un oncle qui aide son neveu à construire son propre chalet;
* travail à distance (par téléphone ou Internet) fait par un résident temporaire dont l’employeur est à l’extérieur du Canada et qui est rémunéré de l’extérieur du Canada;
* travail indépendant où le travail à faire n’aurait aucun impact réel sur le marché du travail, et ne fournirait pas vraiment une occasion aux Canadiens (par exemple, un fermier américain qui traverse la frontière pour travailler sur des champs qu’il possède, ou un mineur venant travailler dans sa propre concession);
- * échanges à court terme d’étudiants du secondaire effectués dans le cadre d’ententes internationales, comme la Commission mixte de coopération régionale entre le Canada atlantique et l’archipel de Saint Pierre et Miquelon.
Il peut y avoir d’autres types d’emplois à court terme non rémunérés où le travail ne découle pas vraiment de la raison principale pour laquelle une personne est en visite au Canada et ne constitue pas une activité concurrentielle, même si un avantage de valeur mais non monétaire est perçu. Par exemple, si un touriste désire rester dans une ferme familiale et travailler à temps partiel et reçoit en contrepartie le gîte et le couvert durant une courte période (c.-à-d. 1-4 semaines), cette personne ne serait pas considérée comme étant un travailleur. Toutefois, si la période de travail dans la ferme doit dépasser quatre semaines, un permis de travail est requis.
