Regarding the email we sent to you on July 11th, we would like to provide a clarification regarding your question. Please see our corrected response to your question. *** For a genuine job offer in TEER 3 or 4, your work experience must be in TEER 2, 3 or 4. In the example provided, the applicant's work experience as NOC 62020 falls under TEER 2 and the applicant's job offer as NOC 63200 falls under TEER 3.
In that example and following the Ministerial Instructions section 5 (1) -see highlighted section- the applicant would be able to apply provided that their work experience totals a minimum of 1560 within the last 3 years when applying and that they satisfy all the other requirements.
Required work experience
5 (1) Subject to subsections (3) and (4), the applicant must demonstrate that they have the following work experience:
- (a) for a genuine offer of employment in TEER Category 0, work experience in an occupation in TEER Category 0, 1, 2 or 3;
- (b) for a genuine offer of employment in TEER Category 1, work experience in an occupation in TEER Category 0, 1, 2 or 3;
- (c) for a genuine offer of employment in TEER Category 2, work experience in an occupation in TEER Category 1, 2, 3 or 4;
- (d) for a genuine offer of employment in TEER Category 3, work experience in an occupation in TEER Category 2, 3 or 4 unless subsection (3) applies;
- (e) for a genuine offer of employment in TEER Category 4, work experience in an occupation in TEER Category 2, 3 or 4 unless subsection (3) applies; and
- (f) for a genuine offer of employment in TEER Category 5, work experience in the same National Occupational Classification unit group as the offer.
All applications are under Officer's discretion, who need to be satisfied that the candidate can perform the duties of the job being offered.

In situations where regularly scheduled work throughout the year varies in hours from week to week, for example based on professional regulatory requirements, the officer would determine on a case-by-case basis if the hours declared could be reasonably considered as work experience. Scenario: A student holds a valid study permit that names a specific DLI, such as UBC. On April 30, 2025, UBC approves a retroactive withdrawal from all courses for the Winter 2025 term (January-April 2025). The student's transcript will reflect no course enrollment as of January 6, 2025, the official start of the term.
Questions:
1. 1. Under IRPR 222(1)(a.1), would this retroactive withdrawal impact the validity of the student's study permit?
2. 2. If so, from which date would IRCC consider the student to have ceased complying with the conditions of their study permit, the date the withdrawal was approved (April 30, 2025), or the retroactively applied date of non-enrollment (January 6, 2025)?

QUESTION:
1. 1. Under IRPR 222(1)(a.1), would this retroactive withdrawal impact the validity of the student's study permit?
2. 2. If so, from which date would IRCC consider the student to have ceased complying with the conditions of their study permit, the date the withdrawal was approved (April 30, 2025), or the retroactively applied date of non- enrolIment (January 6, 2025)?
RESPONSE:
1. Yes. Under R222(1)(a.1), which became effective on November 8, 2024, the study permit becomes invalid on the day on which the permit holder is no longer enrolled at the DLi named in the permit, other than as a result of completing their studies.
2. If the study permit holder remained in Canada but stopped attending classes without notifying the DLl, their study permit would remain valid but they may be found non-compliant with the conditions of that permit (R220.1(1). If they remained in Canada and requested a special dispensation from the DLI to permit them to withdraw from courses late, the study permit would become invalid on the day that request is approved by the DLI (R222(1)(a.1). They would no longer be authorized to study -and may have no status in Canada as of the day they ceased to be enrolled.

Bonjour,
Merci d’avoir contacté la boîte aux courriels pour les représentants en immigration. Veuillez noter que cette boîte aux lettres est destinée à fournir des conseils généraux et ne fournit pas de réponses à des demandes spécifiques à un cas, mais a fourni les informations suivantes comme conseil. Si vous avez des questions spécifiques à un dossier, nous vous encourageons à soumettre le formulaire Formulaire Web d'IRCC-Canada.ca Veuillez consulter notre réponse à votre question.
Question 1 : La présente a pour objet que vous nous confirmiez qu’un travailleur étranger temporaire détenant un Permis de Travail sous le programme TET (avec ElMT-CAQ) peut poursuivre son emploi et n’est pas tenu d’obtenir un nouveau Permis de travail si son nouvel employeur rencontre les critères de la définition d’employeur ‘ayant droit', tel qu’indiquée au site
d'IRCC de Nouvelle dénomination de l'employeur et restructurations d'entreprise-Canada.ca, qui sont :
1. 1. Le nouvel employeur assume les intérêts et les obligations et gère l’actif et le passif de l’ancien employeur;
2. 2. Le nouvel employeur continue d’exercer le même type d’activités que l’ancien employeur;
3. 3. Le nouvel employeur assume le contrat de l’EIMT de l’ancien employeur; et,
4. 4. Les conditions de travail du travailleur indiquées dans l’offre d’emploi au départ, comme le salaire, les fonctions, le lieu de travail, demeurent les mêmes.
Réponse 1 :
Si la société remplaçante est un employeur « ayant droit » en ce sens qu’elle a démontré qu’elle assume, dans une large mesure, les intérêts et les obligations, qu’elle gère l’actif et le passif de la société d’origine (en tout ou en partie) et qu’elle continue d’exercer le même type d’activités que cette dernière, la société remplaçante demeure l’« employeur » en ce qui concerne les permis de travail existants.
Le travailleur temporaire n’a pas à obtenir un nouveau permis de travail et il demeure autorisé à travailler au Canada pendant toute la durée de la période indiquée sur le permis qu’il détient, si :
- * la société remplaçante satisfait aux exigences liées à l’émission du permis de travail dispensé de l’EIMT (p. ex. lien admissible dans le cas d’une mutation à l’intérieur d’une société) ou elle assume le contrat de l’EIMT; •* les conditions de travail du travailleur indiquées dans l’offre d’emploi au départ, comme le salaire, les fonctions, le lieu de travail, demeurent les mêmes.
Pour plus d'informations, veuillez voir le site web ici : Nouvelle dénomination de l’employeur et restructurations d'entreprise-Canada.ca
Question 2 : De plus, prière de nous préciser si cette définition d’employeur ‘ayant droit' s’applique à un propriétaire d’une franchise qui reprends ou rachète celle-ci d’un franchisé en faveur duquel l’EIMT-CAQ et le Permis de travail avaient été émis.
Réponse 2 :
Oui, cette définition d’employeur « ayant droit » s’applique à un propriétaire d’une franchise qui reprends ou rachète celle-ci d’un franchisé, à condition que ce nouvel employeur réponde aux critères de la définition d'un employeur « ayant droit », comme indiqué au site d'IRCC de Restructurations d'entreprise.
Question 3: Également, est-ce que le Franchiseur qui reprend temporairement la franchise d’un propriétaire peut également être qualifié d’employeur ‘ayant droit' s’il rencontre tous les critères énumérés ci-dessus.
Réponse 3:
Oui, cette définition d’employeur « ayant droit » s’applique à un propriétaire d’une franchise qui reprend temporairement une franchise d'un propriétaire, à condition que ce nouvel employeur réponde aux critères de la définition d'un employeur « ayant droit », comme indiqué au site d'IRCC de Restructurations d'entreprise.
Question 4 : En terminant, serait-il possible de nous indiquer la façon à privilégier afin d’informer IRCC et Service Canada d’un nouvel employeur ‘ayant droit'.
Réponse 4:
Dans le cas d’une restructuration d’entreprise, le titulaire de l’EIMT doit communiquer avec Emploi et Développement social Canada (EDSC) et Service Canada (SC) pour les informer du changement. IRCC n’a pas besoin d’être informé du changement.
Pour EDSC, veuillez consulter leur page Web « Communiquer avec le Centre de services aux employeurs ». *** Cordialement,
La boîte aux courriels pour les représentants en immigration

threads.subject: Federal EMPP-Questions on various topics-REP-B-2025-1131 - Due 7-Aug-25
threads.question:
Good dayIRCC,
I have the following questions regarding the Federal Economic Mobility Pathways Pilot.
1. 1. Is it allowed to change jobs while the application for permanent residence is being processed. For example, the person A received a job offer from Company B at the start of their application, but Company B may no longer support the job offer they provided. Person A is notified of this by the employer and looks for another job. If they find another job from Company C, would the regulations concerning Federal EMPP allow for substitution of employers while the application is in process?
2. 2. Hypothetically, a person who is a British citizen who before getting a British citizenship possessed a refugee certificate from the UK government or UNHCR, would that person qualify for Federal EMPP if they produce proof of refugee certificate that was issued to them many years ago?
3. 3. Since there is no option to contact EMPP office by webform as there is no EMPP category in the dropdown menu, which email address should we contact them?
Sincerely,
threads.answer:
Good day,
Thank you for contacting the Immigration Represe ntatives Mailbox. Please note that this mailbox is intended for general guidance and does not provide responses to case-specific inquiries but have provided the following information as guidance. Ifyou have case specific questions about a file, you are encouraged to submit the IRCC Web form.
Please see our response to your question.
*** Question 1: Is it allowed to change jobs while the application for permanent residence is being processed. For example, the person A received a job offer from Company B at the start of their application, but Company B may no longer support the job offer they provided. Person A is notified of this by the employer and looks for another job. If they find another job from Company C, would the regulations concerning Federal EMPP allow for substitution of employers while the application is in process?
Response: If at any point during processing any details change pertaining to a clients EMPP application, they are required to inform the processing office using the webform. If a client loses their job offer, it is their responsibility to promptly inform the processing office. Please note candidates cannot travel to Canada with an expired job offer as they may be refused entry by a CBSA officer for no longer meeting one of the requirements.
If during processing an EMPP client receives a different valid job offer than what they initially applied with, and they would like to proceed with this job offer instead, they can inform the processing office and upload the new job offer through the webform. The onus is always on the applicant to provide sufficient documentation to satisfy an officer that they meet the requirements of the program they are applying under.
Question 2: Hypothetically, a person who is a British citizen who before getting a British citizenship possessed a refugee certificate from the UK government or UNHCR, would that person qualify for Federal EMPP if they produce proof of refugee certificate that was issued to them many years ago?
Response: In order to be eligible under the EMPP, the applicant must show they are a refugee or displaced person. They can demonstrate this through a variety of documents, including a positive Refugee Status Determination (RSD) from the UNHCR or a refugee-hosting state. If an applicant provides an RSD issued from the UNHCR or a refugee-hosting state, they do not need to show their inability to secure a durable solution, or any other criteria related to protection. Please note that the intention of the program is to select refugees and other displaced persons who have the skills and qualifications that Canadian employers need. It is not intended for those who are no longer in need of protection and can qualify under the economic classes.
Question 3: Since there is no option to contact EMPP office by webform as there is no EMPP category in the dropdown menu, which email address should we contact them?
Response: Any question from representatives regarding EMPP operations can be submitted through the Immigration Representative's portal, as was done with this enquiry. Clients can also use the IRCC webform to request the status of their application, update their application, report technical problems or ask about our programs and services. To indicate the query is concerning an EMPP application, under "What did you apply for?" select "Permanent Residence" and under "What
and Citizenshi Canada et Ciloyeneé Canada
application did you submit?" select Federal Skilled Worker. The form requires the client to enter their application number, which will ensure it's connected to the correct EMPP application.
Thank you kindly,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

Response: A long as they meet the other eligibility requirements, students must spend at least 8 months at a Canadian DLi and complete at least 50% of their eligible program in class to be eligible for a PGWP. The length of their PGWP depends on the level and duration of their study program, as well as the expiry date of their passport, whichever comes first. Please note that the current regulation only allows applicants to apply for a PGWP in Canada if their study permit is still valid (not expired) or if they meet one of the other requirements of section R199 at the time they submit their application. If an applicant is eligible for a PGWP and they don't hold a valid study permit, they are eligible to apply from outside Canada. Question 1:
Maintained Status After IEC YP VIE Expiry If a foreign national is under maintained status following the expiry of their IEC Young Professionals (VIE) work permit, are they allowed to continue working for the same employer during the processing period if they are no longer being remunerated by Business France? Response 1:
When applying for a subsequent lEC participation, lEC participants do not meet the requirements for maintained status and are not authorized to work without a permit. Participants may only work while their work permit is valid, regardless if the conditions are the same or not.
Question 2:
Maintained Status After Application for a Different Temporary Resident Status If a foreign national submits an application to change their status (e.g., from worker to visitor) before their work permit
expires, thereby triggering maintained status, are they allowed to continue working under the same conditions of their expired work permit while the new application is being processed? Or must they cease working after their work permit expires and await the decision on their new temporary residence application?
Response 2:
Please note that IRCC cannot provide guidance regarding specific case inquiries or hypothetical scenarios.
An applicant benefits from maintained status if they submit an application to extend or change the conditions of their stay before the expiry date on their status document or, if no status document was issued, before the end of the 6-month period of authorized stay for foreign nationals who entered Canada as a visitor.
If an applicant who previously held a work or study permit applies for a visitor record before the expiry of their permit, they may benefit from maintained status during the processing period of the visitor record application, but they do not have the authorization to work or study after the expiry of their permit. An individual seeking a work or study permit should apply using the process that reflects their physical location, whether that is inside or outside of Canada. Individuals who are inside Canada applying for a work permit using the IMM 1295 – Application for a Work Permit Made Outside of Canada form would have to depart Canada and attempt to re-enter so they can be examined at a port of entry before their work permit can be issued.
As announced by the Government of Canada as part of Canadas Border Plan, clients who have received the Letter of Introduction (LOí) while inside Canada cannot flagpole to receive their permit. Clients must leave and re-enter Canada from a country other than United States or St. Pierre and Miquelon to activate their permit.
As posted on our website at Work permit: How to apply-Canada.ca, individuals in the following situations can apply for a work permit from inside Canada:
- *They have a valid study or work permit.
- * Their spouse, common-law partner or parent has a valid study or work permit. •* They're eligible for a post-graduation work permit and their study permit is still valid.
- * They or their spouse, common-law partner or parent has a temporary resident permit that is valid for 6 months or more.
- * They're in Canada and waiting on a decision on an application for permanent residence for the o* spouse and common-law partner in Canada class or overseas family class o* temporary resident permit holder class
- * They made or will make a claim for refugee protection.
- * They've been recognized as a Convention refugee or protected person by the Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada. •* They're allowed to work in Canada without a work permit, but they do need a work permit to work in a different job (this does not apply to business visitors). •* They're a trader, investor, intra-company transferee or professional under the Canada-United States-Mexico Agreement (CUSMA).
The public policy allowing visitors to apply for work permits from within Canada has ended. Under the policy, visitors in Canada could apply for a work permit without having to leave the country. While we cannot provide case-specific recommendations or immigration advice on work permit options for the scenario you describe, please refer to the eligibility requirements for the Open Work Permit for Vulnerable Workers and our Work in Canada webpage in order to determine the work permit options available.
An applicant is eligible for another OWP-V only if their previous employer-specific work permit is still valid (that is, it has not been revoked and is not invalid under section R209) or they have maintained status on their employer-specific work permit, and they continue to meet the other requirements of section R207.1, meaning they are in Canada, and officers have reasonable grounds to believe they are still experiencing abuse or are at risk of experiencing abuse in the context of their employment in Canada.
An OWP-V is an open work permit that allows the holder to work for almost any employer in Canada for a specified period, except for one that
* is listed as ineligible on the list of employers who have failed to comply with the conditions or
- * regularly offers strip tease, erotic dance, escort services or erotic massages
However, an OWP-V may be restricted in certain circumstances, which would limit the occupation or location of work, for example where the applicant does not have a valid immigration medical examination (IME). Foreign nationals who hold OWP-Vs are still subject to the general conditions imposed on all temporary residents under subsection 183(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR).
For more information, please visit the public instruction here: Open work permit for vulnerable workers who are victims of abuse-Canada.ca and the publicly available instruction for officers at Open work permits for vulnerable workers [R207.1– A72] -International Mobility Program (IMP) - Canada.ca.

If the applicant applied for a new study permit before exiting Canada and returns to Canada without being in possession of a valid study permit, then they do not meet the conditions under section 189 of the regulations and thus, may not resume their studies until authorization to study is granted through issuance of a valid study permit. threads.answer:
Good day, Thank you for contacting the Immigration Representatives Mailbox. Please note that this mailbox is intended for general guidance and does not provide responses to case-specific inquiries but have provided the following information as guidance. Ifyou have case specific questions about a file, you
are encouraged to submit the IRCC Web form.
Please see our response to your question. *** Section 1 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR) define a common-law partner as follows:
common-law partner means, in relation to a person, an individual who is cohabiting with the person in
a conjugal relationship, having so cohabited for a period of at least one year.
Interpretation — common-law partner
(2) For the purposes of the Act and these Regulations, an individual who has been in a conjugal relationship with a person for at least one year but is unable to cohabit with the person, due to persecution or any form of penal control, shall be considered a common-law partner of the person.
When it comes to spousal sponsorships, the Spousal Guide (IMM5289) specifies that a common-law partner means a person who has been living in a conjugal relationship with another person continuously for at least one year. A conjugal relationship exists when there is a significant degree of commitment between two people. This can include sharing the same home; supporting each other financially and emotionally; having children together (if applicable); presenting themselves in public as a couple etc.
For spousal sponsorships, the onus is on the applicant to prove that they have being living together in a common-law relationship for at least one year before an application is received by IRCC, as section 121 of the IRPR states that a person who is a member of the family class who makes an application under Division 6 of Part 5 must be a family member of the sponsor both at the time the application is made and at the time of the determination of the application.
After the one year period of cohabitation has been established, the partners may live apart for periods of time while still maintaining a common-law relationship. For example, a couple may have been separated due to illness or death of a family member, adverse country conditions (e.g. war, political unrest), or employment or education-related reasons, and therefore are not cohabiting at the time an application is submitted. Despite the break in cohabitation, a common-law relationship exists if the couple has cohabited continuously in a conjugal relationship in the past for at least one year and intend to do so again as soon as possible. There should be evidence demonstrating that both parties are continuing the relationship
Lnmn That being said, for common-law relationships, the longer the period of separation without any cohabitation, the more difficult it is to establish that the common-law relationship still exists.
It should be noted that if the applicant is applying under the Spouse and Common-law Partner in Canada class (SCLPC), there is also the requirement under R124(a) of the IRPR that a foreign national cohabits with their sponsor in Canada:
124 A foreign national is a member of the spouse or common-law partner in Canada class if they
(a) are the spouse or common-law partner of a sponsor and cohabit with that sponsor in Canada;
This requirement applies from the date the application is locked-in until the applicant becomes a Permanent Resident.
For temporary resident purposes, the definition of common-law partner under R1(1) applies.
IRCC Officers must continue to be satisfied that the partners are in a bona fide (genuine) relationship and will assess each case individually based on the specific circumstances of the applicant and evidence provided in order to determine whether an applicant is a member of the class under which they have applied and that they meet the eligibility requirements, including the criteria mentioned above. The onus is on the applicant to prove that they have been living common-law for at least one year before an application is received by IRCC and to include relevant details and evidence regarding their particular circumstances. There is no guarantee that a case will be approved.
We hope you find this information useful.

It is critical to note that a person who wishes to sponsor a member of the family class is required to reside in Canada, as per paragraph R130(1)(b). A Canadian adoptive parent who resides abroad and has adopted a child outside Canada may be exempt from the requirement to reside in Canada, according to subsection R130(2), if they satisfy immigration officials that they will reside in Canada once their adopted child becomes a permanent resident in Canada. This exemption does not apply to sponsors who are permanent residents, as they are required to reside in Canada to be eligible to sponsor. This exception applies to adopted children who meet the definition of a dependent child under section R2. A sponsor of a child intended to be adopted in Canada does not qualify for the exceptions in subsection R130(2), as the child does not meet the definition of a dependent child.
Where the adopted child is related to the adoptive parents, the pre-existing legal parent-child relationship should be severed under the law. Evidence that the biological parent(s) fully comprehend the effects of a full adoption and that they have provided their consent to the adoption should also support a determination that the requirements of the IRPA and IRPR have been met. Please refer to how to apply and sponsor your adopted child for more information.

* 181 (1) A foreign national may apply for an extension of their authorization to remain in Canada as a temporary resident if

Could you please confirm whether payments made to a sponsored as a result of WorkSafeBC claim are considered social assistance payments for the undertaking purposes and whether they would need to be repaid by the sponsor?
WorkSafeBC is a provincial agency that administers mandatory workplace insurance ([https://www.worksafebc.com/en/claims/report-workplace-injury-illness/mental-health-injury-claims](https://www.worksafebc.com/en/claims/report-workplace-injury-illness/mental-health-injury-claims))

*** The Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR) define social assistance as:
any benefit in the form of money, goods or services provided to or on behalf of a person by a province under a program of social assistance, including a program of social assistance designated by a province to provide for basic requirements including food, shelter, clothing, fuel, utilities, household supplies, personal requirements and health care not provided by public health care, including dental care and eye care.
WorkSafeBC (WSBC) provides compensation for work-related injuries or illnesses, including wage-loss benefits and health care costs. These benefits are funded through employer-paid insurance premiums, which are calculated based on the employer's size, risk of the work, and injury history. WSBC is not funded through income support programs or general provincial revenues.
As such, WSBC benefits are not considered social assistance by the province of British Columbia, and therefore do not fall under the definition of social assistance used by IRCC for the purposes of sponsorship under the Family Class.
If a sponsored person receives WSBC benefits, the sponsor is not obligated to repay those amounts under the terms of the sponsorship undertaking.

Question 1:
L’un de nos clients, une organisation à but non lucratif, envisage de transférer son siège social au Canada. Dans ce contexte, il souhaite obtenir des précisions sur les possibilités de relocalisation de ses employés.
Plus précisément, nous aimerions savoir : Le transfert du siège social au Canada permet-il également le transfert de certains employés de l’organisation ? Nous pensons notamment au programme des personnes mutées à l’intérieur d’une société (PMIS), qui permet aux entreprises multinationales ayant une entité liée au Canada de transférer temporairement des employés sans exigence d’ElMT, à condition qu’ils aient travaillé au sein de l’entreprise étrangère pendant au moins un an au cours des trois dernières années. Selon les informations dont nous disposons, le volet C-63 du PMIS ne semble pas applicable ici, car les employés ne possèdent pas un niveau avancé d’expertise ou de connaissances exclusives liées aux produits, services, techniques ou à la gestion de l’organisation. Pour déterminer l’admissibilité au volet des personnes mutées à l’intérieur d’une société, les critères d’admissibilité doivent être examinés, notamment
* occuper actuellement un poste de cadre, de gestionnaire, ou posséder des connaissances spécialisées au sein d’une entreprise d'une multinationale à l’extérieur du Canada; o * l’entreprise à l’extérieur du Canada doit faire des affaires au Canada, ou le fera si le demandeur à l’intention d’établir une nouvelle entreprise admissible
Cette catégorie vise à faciliter le déplacement de travailleurs hautement spécialisés qui possèdent un niveau avancé d’expertise et de connaissances exclusives concernant les produits, les services, la recherche, l’équipement, les techniques ou la gestion de l’entreprise.
Personnes mutées à l'intérieur d'une société (PMIS) -[R205a) -C61, C62, C63] -Intérêts canadiens -Programme de mobilité internationale, l’instruction indique « Important : Cette catégorie du Programme de mobilité internationale n’a pas pour but de muter la main-d’œuvre générale d’une entreprise à des entités affiliées au Canada. »
Question 2:
Dans le cadre du programme d’emploi réciproque (C-20), est-il obligatoire que des Canadiens soient déjà employés à l’international au sein de la même organisation ? Est-il possible de conclure une entente entre IRCC et l’organisation pour faciliter ce type de transfert ?
Réponse à la question 2:
Il n’est pas obligatoire que les Canadiens soient déjà employés à l’étranger au sein de la même organisation en vertu du C20.
En vertu du R205b), les travailleurs étrangers peuvent occuper un emploi au Canada là où il existe des possibilités réciproques semblables pour les Canadiens à l’étranger. L’admission accordée en vertu des dispositions de réciprocité devrait avoir une incidence neutre sur le marché du travail.
Il incombe aux établissements ou aux demandeurs de fournir la preuve de l’existence d’une situation de réciprocité. Cela pourrait être indiqué dans l’accord d’échange liant la partie canadienne et la partie étrangère ou, à défaut, dans une lettre de l’établissement canadien qui accueillera l’intéressé ou dans un contrat de travail (si ledit document prouve la réciprocité). threads.question:
Hello IRCC Team:
I hope this email finds you well. I am writing to request a policy clarification regarding the field of study requirement for the Post-Graduation Work Permit (PGWP).
The IRCC website states the following concerning how an applicant can meet the field of study requirement: "You must graduate from a program that's on the list of currently eligible Classification of Instructional Programs (CIP) codes when you submit your study permit application or PGWP application ...If your CIP code is not on the list of currently eligible codes when you apply for a PGWP, it may still be eligible based on when you submitted your study permit application."

4. 4. In December 2024, the student applies for a study permit extension. This is the first application submitted to IRCC that explicitly names the new academic program. The extension is subsequently approved.
The ambiguity lies in interpreting the phrase "when you submit your study permit application". My specific question for policy clarification is:
In the scenario described above, which application date is used to determine eligibility for a future PGWP application for the academic program?
- * Is it the date of the initial study permit application (which was for a foundational, non-PGWP eligible program)?
- * Or, is it the date of the study permit extension application from December 2024 (at which point the academic program was no longer on the eligible CIP code list)?
Students began their academic program while they were PGWP-eligible. The interpretation of this policy will determine if they are rendered ineligible for a PGWP due to a policy change that occurred after they had already commenced their studies.

threads.answer:

Pour conserver leur admissibilité en vertu de l’exemption, les étudiants doivent soumettre leur demande de PTPD dans les 180 jours suivant la réception de la confirmation officielle de l’achèvement de leur programme d’études, en plus de respecter les autres critères d'admissibilité.

The new employer doesn't need to submit a new offer of employment and the worker doesn't need a new work permit if both of the following apply: both companies (the original employer and the new employer) run the same type of business
- * none of the work permit conditions change, including the following:
0 * wages
o * job duties
。 * work location

In this case, the new employer will need to either submit a new offer of employment for each worker or get a Labour Market Impact Assessment (LMIA) (if the job is not LMIA-exempt). These workers can't keep working until they get their new work permits. threads.subject: Can common-law partners submit PR application under the same category independently? - REP-B-2025-1856 - Due 30-Oct-25
threads.question:
To whom it may concern,
I understand that in most cases married couples and common-law partners are recommended to file a PR application as a family such that one of them will be the principal applicant while the other will be the dependent. However, if the common-law partners want to apply for PR on their own merits such that their chance of approval won't be affected by a change in their relationship in the future, is that possible? To provide more context, an example is a PR application under the public policy for Hong Kong residents, a common-law couple may want to file their own PR application independently without declaring their common-law partnership, which I know would put them at risk of misrepresentation. However, once the common-law partnership is declared they would need to file a joint PR application. Given the deadline of the public policy is coming up in Aug 2026, if there is a change in their relationship in the future, the dependent in the application would lose the chance of filing another independent application. So, is there a legal way to tackle this issue?
Thank you. Regards,
threads.answer:
Good afternoon,
As you've correctly noted, not declaring a common law relationship would be considered misrepresentation.
Applicants can have multiple applications for PR open at the same time. They can have an application in the SCLP class as well as an application in the HK Public Policy stream. They would have to pay fees for both, but it would be possible to keep both applications open while they're being processed. When/if PRis received the other application would be cancelled and there would be no refund for the processing fees.
If both applicants qualify for and are applying through the Hong Kong Public Policy stream they could both apply separately and declare the other spouse as non-accompanying. That way they would both have their own application and it would not be affected by their potential future relationship status.

Question A) : If a Canadian corporation and the attendant applicants applying for permanent residence who are being supported by a government-approved Incubator that is not listed as a priority designated organization referenced above, from the current inventory of pending applications for permanent residence under the start up business class, that were submitted prior to April 30, 2024, receives a term sheet from the incubator for a $75,000 investment commitment, would such a commitment qualify as "committed capital" as defined in the relevant operational bulletin? Further, would this result in the applicants associated with the commitment certificate, being supported by the Incubator, receiving prioritization by ClO?
Answer : Yes, this application would be considered prioritized under the current Start-Up Visa prioritization:
Although the incubator is not part of Canada's Tech Network (CTN), the $75,000 investment commitment meets the capital threshold required for prioritization. Specifically: Angel investor groups and venture capital funds need only show they have committed the required amount of capital to the applicant's business; there is no additional prioritization screening, so almost all applicants they sponsor are automatically prioritized.
For business incubators, prioritization depends on whether the incubator is part of the CTN:
oIf the incubator is in the CTN, applicants are automatically prioritized. 0If the incubator is not in the CTN, applicants can still be prioritized if they have secured at least $75,000 in committed capital.
Since this scenario meets the second condition, it qualifies for prioritization even if the application was submitted before April 30, 2024.
Question B) : If a Canadian corporation and the attendant applicants applying for permanent residence who are being supported by a government-approved Incubator that is not listed as a priority designated organization referenced above, from the current inventory of pending applications for permanent residence under the start up business class, that were submitted prior to April 30, 2024, receives a term sheet for a $75,000 investment commitment from an approved Angel Investor group identified in the above list, would such a commitment qualify as "committed capital" as defined in the relevant operational bulletin? Further, would this result in the
applicants associated with the commitment certificate, being supported by an Incubator, receiving prioritization by the CIO under the Start-Up Visa Program?
Answer : Yes, this application would be prioritized under the current Ministerial Instructions for the Start-Up Business Class. Specifically:
- A $75,000 investment commitment from a designated Angel Investor group qualifies as “committed capital” according to the Ministerial Instructions. The application does not need support from a CTN-member incubator to be prioritized since the prioritization is based on the angel investor's commitment.
These instructions apply to all applications, including those submitted before April 30, 2024, as long as the commitment meets the specified criteria.
The Ministerial Instructions state that all Start-Up Business Class applications, including those submitted before the effective date, will be prioritized if supported by a commitment that meets certain conditions—one being a minimum investment of $75,000 from an authorized angel investor group. Therefore, your application meets the prioritization criteria, and the CiO will prioritize it accordingly.
Please be advised that the assessment of each application is done on a case-by-case basis, taking into account the specific circumstances and supporting documentation provided. It is the applicant's responsibility to ensure that sufficient documentation is submitted to demonstrate compliance with the program's requirements.

J’espère que vous allez bien en ce début de session fort occupé au point de vue de l’immigration.
Je vous écris afin de clarifier des informations concernant les étudiants qui passent du secondaire au cégep pour la session d’automne 2025.
Des étudiants qui étaient au secondaire l’an dernier et qui entrent au cégep à l’automne 2025, nous confirment que des agents d’IRCC leur ont dit qu’ils pouvaient commencer leurs études au cégep sans avoir reçu leur permis d’études, dans certaines circonstances, par exemple si l’étudiant possède une fiche visiteur. Ce n’est pas l’information que nous retrouvons sur le site d’IRCC.
Afin de bien conseiller nos étudiants, j’aimerais vérifier auprès de vous si les étudiants dans les situations suivantes peuvent légalement commencer leurs études au cégep pour la session d’automne 2025, selon les documents d'immigration qu'ils disposent ?
1. L'étudiant provenant du secondaire possède :
- permis d'études du secondaire sans la mention "doit étudier au primaire ou au secondaire"-
- CAQ collégial

- Il n’a pas reçu son nouveau permis d’études Est-ce que l’étudiant peut commencer ses études au cégep à la session d’automne 2025 ?
2. L'étudiant provenant du secondaire possède :
- permis d'études du secondaire avec la mention "doit étudier au primaire ou au secondaire"-
- CAQ collégial
- Il a déposé une demande de prolongation de son permis d'études avant l’expiration de celui-ci
- Il n’a pas reçu son nouveau permis d’études Est-ce que l’étudiant peut commencer ses études au cégep à la session d’automne 2025 ?
3. L'étudiant provenant du secondaire possède :
- fiche visiteur
- CAQ collégial
- Il a déposé une demande de permis d'études
- Il n’a pas reçu son permis d’études Est-ce que l’étudiant peut commencer ses études au cégep à la session d’automne 2025 ?

Bonjour,
Merci d’avoir contacté la boîte aux courriels pour les représentants en immigration.
Veuillez noter que cette boîte aux lettres est destinée à fournir des conseils généraux et ne fournit pas de réponses à des demandes spécifiques à un cas, mais a fourni les informations suivantes comme conseil. En réponse à vos questions numérotées 1 et 2, veuillez noter que les étudiants qui passent du niveau secondaire au niveau postsecondaire doivent obtenir un permis d'études pour les études postsecondaires en présentant une demande pour faire prolonger leur séjour au Canada à titre d'étudiant (prolongation du permis d'études). Une fois leur demande présentée, ils peuvent poursuivre leurs études au niveau postsecondaire en attendant la décision concernant leur nouvelle demande de permis d'études. Si leur demande de permis d'études est refusée, ils doivent cesser immédiatement leurs études. Si toutefois, leur permis d'études mentionne un établissement d'enseignement désigné (EED) spécifique, ils doivent attendre que leur demande de permis d'études soit approuvée avant de commencer leurs études.
En réponse votre question numérotée 3, les étudiants qui étaient admissibles à étudier au niveau secondaire avec une fiche visiteur doivent également demander un permis d'études pour pouvoir étudier au niveau postsecondaire en soumettant une demande pour faire prolonger leur séjour au Canada à titre d'étudiant. Veuillez noter qu'ils ne peuvent pas commencer leurs études au niveau postsecondaire tant que leur permis d'études n'a pas été approuvé.
Nous espérons que ces informations vous seront utiles.
Cordialement,
La boîte aux courriels pour les représentants en immigration

Les directives indiquent : Il est possible que l’étudiant souhaite ou doive interrompre temporairement ses études pendant son séjour au Canada. Lorsqu’il s’agit d’évaluer si l’étudiant poursuit activement ses études, tout congé d’un programme d’études au Canada ne doit pas dépasser 150 jours à compter de la date de début du congé, et le congé doit avoir été autorisé par l’EED.
On considère qu'un étudiant en congé qui commence ou reprend ses études dans les 150 jours qui suivent la date de début du congé (c'est-à-dire la date à laquelle l’établissement lui a accordé un congé) poursuit activement ses études pendant son congé. Si l’étudiant ne reprend pas ses études dans les 150 jours, il doit suivre un des 2 scénarios suivants :
changer son statut (c'est-à-dire changer pour un statut de visiteur ou un statut de travailleur); quitter le Canada.
S’il ne change pas son statut ou ne quitte pas le Canada, il est réputé non conforme aux conditions liées à son permis d’études.
Les étudiants qui cessent leurs études et ne sont pas autorisés par leur établissement d'enseignement désigné à prendre congé peuvent être considérés comme ne respectant pas les conditions de leur permis d'études. Ce manquement peut avoir une incidence négative sur leur future demande. Par exemple, un permis de travail subséquent pourrait ne pas être délivré avant six mois, après la cessation des études non autorisées ou le non- respect d'une condition, conformément à l'alinéa 221a) et au sous-alinéa R200(3)(e)(i).

As indicated on our website, the amount of work experience that was required is based on when IRCC assesses the application, which means the most recent change in the work experience requirement to 6 months applies to all applications pending a final decision, regardless of when the application was submitted.
For example:
- If an applicant submits their proof of work experience after June 16, 2024, they would only be required to submit proof of at least 6 months of experience, regardless of when they applied or when the Stage 1 decision (pre- assessment of permanent residence eligibility and issuance of the occupation-restricted open work permit) had been made.
- If an application was refused on June 1, 2024 because the applicant didn't have sufficient work experience (i.e., 12 months), the application would not be re-opened on June 17th and re-assessed for 6 months of work experience, since at the time a decision was made on the application, the requirement was 12 months.
- If an applicant submitted their proof of work experience when the required experience was 12 months, but IRCC assessed that proof after June 16, 2024, they would be assessed for 6 months. For applications submitted under the Gaining experience category, the work experience can be either from within Canada or overseas. Any work experience gained in Canada must be authorized. The work can be authorized under any combination of authorized work permits or authorizations, acquired while the applicant had temporary resident status, as long as the applicant was not engaged in full-time study. This means that the work experience can be from a work permit issued under the International Mobility Program or the Temporary Foreign Worker Program, including a post- graduate work permit (PGWP), Live-in Caregiver program (LCP) work permit, work permits issued under the International Experience Canada (IEC) program (e.g., working holiday work permit), etc. For the Gaining experience category applications, while experience gained on any work authorizations outside of the occupation-restricted open work permit (OROWP) can count, the deadline for submitting proof of work experience is still 36 months following OROWP issuance.
As applicants are now able to use Canadian or foreign work experience, or a combination of both, to satisfy the work experience requirement, they may have 6 months of work experience that they obtained before they were even issued an OROWP that is now eligible. However, eligible work experience must have been accumulated no more than 36 months before the initial application was submitted. For example, if an applicant submitted their application for permanent residence on June 1, 2021, they can only use eligible work experience obtained after June 1, 2018 (and up to 36 months after issuance of the OROWP). In all cases, it is important that the applicant carefully reviews all documentation to ensure they meet the work experience requirement before sending their proof, as a decision will be made based on the information that is provided.
For applications submitted under the direct to permanent residence category (Category B), the work experience can only be Canadian, and obtained within the 36 months before the application was submitted.
For more information, refer to our website:

Students engaging in post-secondary studies in Canada are authorized to pursue programs of study within the same DLl, provided they are not limited from doing so by conditions imposed on their study permit, and they have submitted an application to change conditions, extend their stay or remain in Canada as a student before their current study permit expired. They should begin or resume their studies in their new program within 150 days from the day that they ceased or completed their studies at the previous program if they are within Canada. If a student does not resume their studies within 150 days, they should do either of the following: change their status (that is, change to visitor status or worker status), or leave Canada.

For International Experience Canada (lEC), if a temporary resident applies for a work permit renewal (extension) in a category outside of the lEC program while their lEC work permit is still valid, they receive the authorization to work without a permit under paragraph R186(u), and the conditions of their lEC work permit continue until a decision is made. This period of time when they are authorized to work without a permit is not considered an extension of their IEC participation.
If the temporary foreign worker is renewing with the same employer but different conditions, paragraph R186(u) applies and they are authorized to work; however, while waiting for a decision, the worker must continue to comply with the original conditions.
Pursuant to subsection R209.2(2), the period of employment for the employer conditions listed in section 209.2 includes any period during which the temporary resident was authorized to work under paragraph R186(u) after the expiry of their work permit. Therefore, the employer continues to be subject to the conditions and may be subject to inspection until a decision is made on the subsection R201(1) application. This does not necessarily mean the salary must be exactly the same, rather, as per R209.2(1)(jii), the employer must provide the foreign national with employment in the same occupation as that set out in the foreign national's offer of employment and with wages and working conditions that are substantially the same as — but not less favourable than — those set out in that offer.
See Pending decision on work permit renewal [R186(u)]: Authorization to work without a work permit-International Mobility Program (IMP) - Canada.ca for more information.

Dear IRCC,
I am writing as the authorized legal representative for my clients, a couple currently residing in Canada. The sponsor is a naturalized Canadian citizen, and the applicant is the sponsored spouse in an ongoing inland spousal sponsorship process.
The couple is planning to travel to for the birth of their baby, which is due in December 2025. They intend to remain in Colombia for only a few months and return to Canada together with the baby.

Specifically, we seek clarification on the following:
1. If the child is born abroad and obtains Canadian citizenship by descent, would there be any requirement to include her in the ongoing sponsorship process?
2. If the clients decide to change their current inland spousal sponsorship to an outland application due to temporary travel, would this require submitting a new application and losing the progress already made?
3. For an outland spousal sponsorship, if the applicant leaves Canada temporarily and plans to return within a few months with the Canadian sponsor and their newborn, would there be any implications for re-entry or the continuation of the process?
We appreciate your guidance so we can advise our clients on the most appropriate course of action.

threads.answer:
October 9, 2025 11:51 AM
FW: (CPD-2025-0539) FW: Request for Guidance – Proof of Citizenship vs. Sponsorship
Good day,
Thank you for contacting the Immigration Representatives Mailbox.
Please note that this mailbox is intended for general guidance and does not provide responses to case-specific inquiries but have provided the following information as guidance. If you have case specific questions about a file, you are encouraged to submit the RCC Web form.
Please see our response to your question.
1. Based on our understanding, the child may be eligible for Canadian citizenship by descent. My clients wish to confirm whether applying for a Proof of Citizenship and subsequently a Canadian passport would make it unnecessary to include the child in the sponsorship application.
A child born overseas to a Canadian citizen parent may be eligible for citizenship by descent, provided certain conditions are met. See Check if you may be a citizen and Am I a Canadian? for more information.
Generally, if the Canadian citizen parent was either born in Canada or became a naturalized Canadian citizen before the child was born, the child is likely eligible for Canadian citizenship by descent. Based on the information provided, this appears to be the likely case however we cannot confirm citizenship status for an unborn child, especially as the rules for citizenship by descent are changing.
The child's parents are encouraged to apply for proof of Canadian citizenship once the child is born, as this is the formal way to find out if a person is a citizen. Should the parents choose to proceed via the citizenship route, there would be no need to include the child in the immigration sponsorship application; however, they must provide proof of citizenship (a citizenship certificate) when applying for the child's passport. It is important to note that the parents should apply for the child's Canadian citizenship documentation before attempting to travel to Canada, as it serves as the official proof that they are a Canadian citizen. Furthermore, Canadian citizens can no longer travel to Canada by air with a non-Canadian passport. See Dual Canadian citizens need a valid Canadian passport for more information.
If it is determined that the child does not have a claim to citizenship by descent, the parents may still choose to sponsor their child as a permanent resident under the IRPA and apply for Canadian citizenship at a later date.
1. If the child is born abroad and obtains Canadian citizenship by descent, would there be any requirement to include her in the ongoing sponsorship process?
As noted above, there would be no requirement to include the child in the spousal sponsorship application as a dependent, if the parents are choosing to submit a citizenship application.
中 et Cioyenneté Canada
2. If the clients decide to change their current inland spousal sponsorship to an outland application due to temporary travel, would this require submitting a new application and losing the progress already made?
Applicants applying under the overseas family class stream or Spouse or Common-Law Partner in Canada class (SCLPC) stream must meet the requirements of the stream under which they've applied throughout the application process. As both streams have different requirements, it would not be possible to convert the application from the overseas to the in-Canada stream or vice versa. Generally, a sponsor should apply under the Family Class if the person they want to sponsor currently lives with them in Canada, but does not plan to stay in Canada while the application is being processed. Should the sponsor and the principal applicant decide to change their Spouse or Common-Law Partner in Canada (SCLPC) application to a Family Class application, the SCLPC application would have to be withdrawn and a new application submitted.
Applicants applying under the spouse or common-law partner in Canada class must cohabit with their sponsor in Canada. As noted in the Complete Guide, leaving Canada can automatically cancel temporary resident status as a visitor, student or worker. If the applicant leaves Canada before becoming a permanent resident, they may not be allowed to come back. This is especially true if they need a Temporary Resident Visa or an eTA to enter Canada. The border services officer at the port of entry will determine whether a foreign national is authorized to enter Canada. If your spouse or partner can't return to Canada, they will not longer meet the requirements of the in Canada class and they will need to submit a new overseas sponsorship application.
3. For an outland spousal sponsorship, if the applicant leaves Canada temporarily and plans to return within a few months with the Canadian sponsor and their newborn, would there be any implications for re-entry or the continuation of the process
As there is no requirement under the overseas family class for an applicant to be in or remain in Canada, leaving Canada during the processing of the spousal sponsorship application would not have an impact on their eligibility under the family class. That said, if an applicant applying under the overseas Family Class is in Canada, they must comply with the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act and Regulations. This includes maintaining their valid temporary resident status while they are in Canada. Failure to do so could result in them being found inadmissible and their application for permanent residence being refused.
There is no guarantee that a foreign national will be allowed to re-enter Canada. The onus is on the applicant to ensure they have the proper documentation required to enter Canada and are not inadmissible. The border services officer at the port of entry will determine whether a foreign national is authorized to enter Canada.
We hope you find this information useful.
Thank you kindly,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

Bonjour,
Nous aimerions savoir si des étudiants qui ont diplômé d’un premier programme d’études peuvent en commencer un 2º en bénéficiant de l’article R189 (étudier sans permis d’études), suite à une demande de prorogation de permis d’études présentée alors que le permis antérieur est devenu invalide par l’application de l’article R222(1)a)?
Voici un exemple de scénario :
Étudiant termine un premier programme avec un permis d’études encore valide pour 6-12 mois après l’obtention du diplôme.
Étudiants présentent la demande (et obtient) le permis de travail postdiplome. Permis d’études devient invalide 90 jours après avoir terminé les études [R222(1)a)]. Étudiant veut retourner aux études (dans le même EED). Étudiant présente une demande de permis d’études, entre le moment où le permis d’études précédent devient invalide et l’expiration de ce dernier. Est-ce que cette demande est considérée comme un renouvellement de son permis d’études présenté avant son expiration [R217]? Ou, est-ce que cette demande est considérée comme une nouvelle demande [R215] malgré le fait que la personne détient un permis d’études non-expiré? ●Si cette demande est considérée comme un renouvellement [R217], peut-il bénéficier du droit d’étudier sans permis d’études en vertu du R189?
Si oui, durant quelle période?
Dès le dépôt de la demande du 2° permis d’études 0Uniquement durant la période entre l’expiration du 1er permis d’études et la réception du 2º permis d’études.
Nous nous posons la question, car l’article R217(1) fait référence à une demande présentée avant l’expiration du permis d’études, mais ne mentionne rien en regard à la validité du dit permis
Un permis peut-il être invalide, mais non expiré, et toujours donner des autorisations en vertu de la LiPR?
Est-ce que votre réponse est différente si l’invalidité du permis découle de l’application de R222(1)a.1) et non du R222(1)a)?
Pouvez-vous confirmer que les conditions auxquelles font référence l’article R189 et l’article R217(1)b) sont celles des articles R183(1), R185 et R220.1 (1)?
Est-ce qu’une personne qui a été diplômée et qu1 détient un permis d’études non-expiré, mais invalide suite à l’application de l’article R222(1)a) est dispensée des conditions de l’article R220.1(1) ?
Merci de votre support
Ghazal, Reda (IRCC/IRCC)
threads.answer:
Bonjour,
Merci d’avoir contacté la boîte aux courriels pour les représentants en immigration.
Veuillez noter que cette boîte aux lettres est destinée à fournir des conseils généraux et ne fournit pas de réponses à des demandes spécifiques à un cas, mais a fourni les informations suivantes comme conseil. Si vous avez des questions spécifiques à un dossier, nous vous encourageons à soumettre le formulaire Formulaire Web d'IRCC-Canada.ca
Veuillez consulter notre réponse à votre question.
Lorsqu'un étudiant diplômé présente une demande de permis d'études après que son permis est devenu invalide en vertu de l’article R222(1)(a), mais avant la date d’expiration officielle du permis, cette demande n’est pas considérée comme une prorogation selon l’article R217, car le permis est invalide, même s’il n’est pas encore expiré. Elle est donc traitée comme une nouvelle demande en vertu de l’article R215. Par conséquent, l’article R189, qui permet à un étudiant de poursuivre ses études sans permis pendant le traitement d’une demande de prorogation valide, ne s’applique pas. L’étudiant ne peut donc pas reprendre ses études tant que le nouveau permis n’a pas été délivré.
Un permis d’études peut être non expiré mais tout de même invalide, notamment en vertu des articles R222(1)(a) ou R222(1)(a.1). Dans ces situations, le permis ne confère plus de statut ni d’autorisation en vertu de la Loi sur l’immigration et la protection des réfugiés.
Enfin, une personne détenant un permis d’études non expiré mais invalide selon R222(1)a) n’est pas exemptée des conditions prévues à l’article R220.1(1) et doit attendre l’approbation d’un nouveau permis avant de pouvoir reprendre ses études.
Cordialement,
La boîte aux courriels pour les représentants en immigration

Age lock-in dates vary by immigration program or category. Whether your child is eligible as a dependant depends on how old they are on that date. For most programs, your child's age lock-in date is the date we get your complete application for permanent residence. Some programs have several steps, so your child's age is locked in before you submit your complete application for permanent residence.
For example, for Home Care Worker Immigration pilot applications, the age of a dependent child is locked in on the date of receipt of the principal applicant's complete permanent residence application. A complete permanent residence application contains all of the items in the document checklist for the specific category, which includes proof of payment of the correct processing fees. The date that IRCC reviews the application for completeness and issues the acknowledgement of receipt (AOR) does not determine the lock-in date.
A child who is less than 22 years of age and not a spouse or common-law partner at the time of “age lock-in” continues to be a dependent child even if they turn 22 during the processing of the application, as long as they are still unmarried and not in a common-law relationship when permanent residence is confirmed. (Less than 22 years means up to and including the last day before the child's 22nd birthday).
A child who is 22 or over and dependent on their parent(s) due to a physical or mental condition is eligible to be processed as a dependant. However, they must continue to be dependent when a final decision is made on the application and when permanent residence in Canada is confirmed.
Please see here for more information about dependent children.

To qualify for the Home Care Worker Immigration pilots, applicants must have enough relevant work experience OR training. Applicants must have either 6 months of continuous, full-time and relevant work experience in the past 3 years OR completed a relevant training credential in the past 2 years before they apply. Please see here for more information regarding qualifying work experience and training. As per paragraph R185(b), an officer may impose specific conditions on a temporary resident, including the work they are both permitted to engage in or prohibited from engaging in while in Canada. If an applicant's work permit has remarks that they are not authorized to work in child care or health services field occupations, any work that they undertake as a home child care provider or home support worker would be considered unauthorized. These conditions would typically be imposed on individuals who have not undergone a medical examination, to ensure they do not take a job that requires close contact with people, such as care for children, the elderly and the disabled, in order to protect public health.
2. Is experience working in a senior care home eligible for the Caregiver Pilot Program that will reopen in 2026? Under the Home Care Worker Immigration Pilot Home Support stream, applicants must have recent and relevant work experience or training. The work experience for the Home Care Worker Immigration Pilots must:
be in 1 or both of the National Occupational Classifications (NOCs) of the pilot they apply for HCWIP: Home Support Home support workers, caregivers and related occupations (NOC 44101) Nurse aides, orderlies and patient service associates (NOC 33102) Work experience in NOC 33102 gained in an institutional setting (for example, long-term care) may be eligible. •Must be in the NOCs of 1 pilot—either child care or home support.
The work experience must match the NoC job description and include most of the main duties listed under the NOC. Please see here for more information regarding work experience.
Applicants must also have a genuine and valid job offer for full-time employment in the home support worker occupation in Canada (NOC 44101) to be eligible. The job offer must demonstrate the applicant will be providing personal care services, not health or nursing services, in a residential setting.
NoC 44101: Home support workers, caregivers and related occupations, provide personal care and companionship for seniors, persons with disabilities and convalescent clients. They provide care in the client's residence, where they may also reside. They are employed by home care and support agencies, private households, or they may be self-employed.
Job offer eligibility depends on the specific nature of the caregiving role. If the caregiving work involves providing personal care services in a residential setting the job offer may qualify. Officers will use all available information to determine whether the applicant will be providing services that align with the NOC and whether the work setting is considered the care recipient's private residence. If the work will extend beyond personal care services and is offered in an institution, it may be ineligible.
Please see here for more information regarding job offers, and here for more information regarding eligible employers.

Le fait de déposer une demande de résidence permanente (RP) pour considérations humanitaires n'empêche pas
une personne de soumettre ultérieurement une demande de RP dans un programme pour travailleurs qualifiés,
même si la première demande est refusée. Il peut s’agir, par exemple, du Programme des travailleurs qualifiés du Québec ou du Programme fédéral des travailleurs qualifiés, dans le cadre d’Entrée express.
Toutefois, il est important de noter que chaque demande est évaluée indépendamment selon les critères du
programme concerné. Si la demande humanitaire est refusée, la personne devra toujours répondre aux exigences
du programme de travailleurs qualifiés choisi, notamment en matière d'expérience professionnelle, de compétences linguistiques et d'autres critères d'admissibilité. Il est également essentiel que la personne ne soit pas visée par une mesure de renvoie exécutoire et qu’elle maintienne un statut de résident temporaire valide au Canada, si elle souhaite y demeurer pendant le traitement de sa nouvelle demande.
Si vous souhaitez plus de précisions, vous pouvez consulter cette ressource sur les demandes de RP Immigrer au Canada-Canada.ca
Veuillez noter que l’évaluation d’une demande est effectuée au cas par cas, en tenant compte des circonstances particulières et des documents justificatifs fournis à l’officier. Bonjour,
Au regard des modifications faites par IRCC en novembre dernier, j’aimerais avoir des précisions sur le cas suivant :
Des étudiants ont dû interrompre leur scolarité temporairement pour des raisons financières, ils ne sont pas admissibles à un congé autorisé par l’EED. Cependant, dans la mesure où ils respectent les conditions pendant leur interruption (maintien d’une assurance maladie et médicaments privée, ne travaillent pas), que la date d’expiration sur le permis d’études est en 2026 ou 2027 et que leur situation financière s’est régularisée, est-il possible pour eux de reprendre les études à la session suivante, avec le même permis d’études? Ainsi, dans le contexte d’un congé d’études non autorisé, est-ce que le permis d’études est encore valide pour reprendre malgré que la date d’expiration indique que oui?
Si le permis devient invalide, qu’elle est la procédure que les étudiants devraient faire pour régulariser leur
statut d’étudiant et être autorisés à reprendre les études? Merci,
Ghazal, Reda (IRCC/IRCC)
threads.answer:
3-Nov-25
Bonjour,
Merci d’avoir contacté la boîte aux courriels pour les représentants en immigration.
Veuillez noter que cette boîte aux lettres est destinée à fournir des conseils généraux et ne fournit pas de réponses à des demandes spécifiques à un cas, mais a fourni les informations suivantes comme conseil. Si vous avez des questions spécifiques à un dossier, nous vous encourageons à soumettre le formulaire Formulaire Web d'IRCC-Canada.ca
Veuillez consulter notre réponse à votre question.
Conformément au paragraphe 220.1(1) du Règlement sur l'immigration et la protection des réfugiés (RIPR), le titulaire d’un permis d’études au Canada est assujetti aux deux conditions suivantes :
a. Il est inscrit à l’établissement d'enseignement désigné (EED) figurant sur son permis d’études et y demeure inscrit jusqu'à ce qu’il termine ses études;
b. Il suit activement son cours ou son programme d’études.
Il est possible que l’étudiant souhaite ou doive interrompre temporairement ses études pendant son séjour au Canada. Lorsqu'il s’agit d’évaluer si l’étudiant poursuit activement ses études, tout congé d’un programme d’études au Canada ne doit pas dépasser 150 jours à compter de la date de début du congé, et le congé doit avoir été autorisé par l’EED. Il doit quitter le Canada s’il ne respecte pas ces conditions et qu’il ne détient pas d’autre autorisation valide, tel qu’un permis de séjour temporaire, une fiche de visiteur, un permis de travail, ou ne dépose pas de demande pour changer de statut (c'est-à-dire changer pour un statut de visiteur ou un statut de travailleur).
Conformément à l’article R222(1)(a.1), un permis d'études devient invalide lorsque le titulaire du permis n'est plus inscrit à l’établissement d’enseignement désigné qui est nommé dans son permis, à moins qu'il n'ait terminé ses études. Si le permis d'études d'un étudiant devient invalide en vertu du paragraphe R222(1) et qu'il ne détient pas d'autre autorisation valide, telle qu'un permis de séjour temporaire, une fiche de visiteur, un permis de travail ou un nouveau permis d'études, il doit quitter le Canada. S'il souhaite revenir, il doit présenter une nouvelle demande depuis l'étranger.
Nous espérons que ces informations vous seront utiles.
Cordialement,
La boîte aux courriels pour les représentants en immigration

1 - 150-Day Gap Rule (General): The IRCC guidelines indicate that a study permit holder must not have a gap exceeding 150 calendar days between the completion of one program and the start of another to remain compliant with the “actively pursue studies” condition. If the gap between the end of one program and the start of the next exceeds 150 days, is the student required to either leave Canada or apply for a Visitor Record to maintain lawful status in Canada?
Response: If a student finishes one program and plans to start another, but the gap between the two exceeds 150 days, they are no longer considered to be actively pursuing studies. In this case, the student must: Leave Canada before the 150-day period ends, or Apply for a Visitor Record to change their status from student to visitor if they wish to remain in Canada during the gap.

2 - Deferred Enrollment and 150 Days: For deferred enrollments, it is understood that the 150-day period may be calculated from the date of the deferral confirmation (e.g., updated Letter of Acceptance or DLl notification) to the start of the next available term. Is this a separate rule from the general 150-day gap between programs, or must both timelines be considered concurrently? For example, if the new intake starts within 150 days of the deferral confirmation but exceeds 150 days from the completion of the previous program, would a Visitor Record be required?
Response: The deferred enrolment counts as authorized leave. If the study permit holder is in Canada at the time of deferral, and they wish to remain in Canada the authorized leave timeframe remains as 150 days. For more information on what counts as authorized leave, please see: Your conditions as a study permit holder in Canada-Canada.ca

their study permit extension application is pending, provided they have a valid Letter of Acceptance and remain enrolled in a DLI?
Response: For students moving from secondary to post-secondary levels, they would need to get a new study permit by applying to extend their current one to attend a post-secondary school. They can continue their studies at the post-secondary level while waiting for a decision on their new study permit application. If their study permit application is refused, they must stop studying immediately.
For more information, please see: Changing your school or program-Canada.ca

Thank you for your enquiry regarding automatic notifications from the Citizenship Application Status Tracker.
The Citizenship Application Status Tracker is built using a one-to-one access model, meaning that access is granted based on the email address associated to the application and the client's Unique Client Identifier (UCl).
When a client or representative creates an account, by entering the UCl and Application number, the Tracker will send a confirmation code by email to the email address associated to the application. If a representative receives the code, it is because someone started the account creation process. If it is a client (assuming they would have the application number which would have been sent to the representative), the representative will receive the confirmation code. A confirmation code is also sent to the email address on file when a client/representative attempts to recover a lost password.
For security reasons, the account registration process cannot be completed without the confirmation code. Also for security reasons, IRCC cannot provide personal information, such as a UCl or application number, with the confirmation code. Only the date and time that the code request was triggered is included for reference as the confirmation code is valid for 24 hours.
If a client using a representative knows their application number, they could initiate the account creation process, which would send the confirmation code to their representative's email address. Information is available, on the Citizenship Application Status Tracker and IRCC help pages, to explain that the confirmation code email will be send to the representative's email address for clients who are using a representative. If a client contacts IRCC because they have not received the confirmation code email, our agents will remind them that the email address associated to their application is that of their representative and to contact their representative to get case status updates.
This is likely the reason why a representative could be receiving the confirmation email without having initiated the account creation process. If this is the case, representatives can ignore the email with the confirmation code.

On December 19, 2023, the Ontario Superior Court of Justice declared that key provisions setting out the first-generation limit for those born abroad are unconstitutional. The Court suspended this declaration until November 20, 2025. To address the Court's decision while upholding the value of Canadian citizenship Bill C-3, An Act to amend the Citizenship Act (2025), was introduced in the House of Commons in order to make changes to the first-generation limit.
Until the period of invalidity to the Court's decision expires and changes to the rules on the first-generation limit to citizenship by descent come into force, the interim measure will remain in place for individuals who are impacted by the first-generation limit. To be considered under the interim measure applicants must complete an application for Citizenship certificate (i.e. proof of citizenship) or Adoption including necessary documentation outlined in the document checklist for the respective applications. Failure to provide a complete application including the necessary documentation may result in the rejection of the application.
Once the changes to the first-generation limit to citizenship by descent are in effect, applications impacted by the first-generation limit for proof or adoption will be processed in accordance with the rules in place at the time of processing and will no longer pass through the interim measure unless it is still applicable at that time. Applicants may choose to wait until the changes are in place to submit their applications – November 20, 2025 must not be viewed as a deadline for application submission rather it is an indication as to how the department handles the processing of the application.

1. If an applicant has valid biometrics on file from a previous application, can these still be used for a new Super Visa application submitted with a newly issued passport? Response: Yes, biometrics from a previous application can be re-used in support of a subsequent application assuming the biometrics are still valid. Please refer to the information below. Here is the link for reference with more information relating to the re-use of biometrics. Biometrics – 1 in 10 expiry periods. Something to keep in mind is the validity of the Visa cannot be issued longer than the expiry of the Passport, or of the biometrics validity – whichever comes first.
Permanent residence applicants
Temporary resident to permanent resident: Valid biometrics provided to support a temporary residence application cannot be reused to support a permanent residence application.
Permanent resident to permanent resident: Biometrics provided to support a permanent residence application cannot be reused to support a subsequent or new permanent residence application. Applicants applying for permanent residence are required to enrol their biometrics to support every permanent residence application.
Permanent residence applicant to temporary residence applicant
Permanent resident to temporary resident: The biometrics can be reused to support a temporary residence application in cases where a foreign national has already provided the biometrics to support a permanent residence application, asylum claim, or overseas refugee resettlement application and is waiting for a decision on that application or claim.
2. Could the remaining validity period of the biometrics significantly reduce the validity or duration granted for the new Super Visa?
Citoyenneté Canada
Response: Yes, the remaining validity period of biometrics can affect the duration of the Visa. Canada cannot issue a visa or permit that extends beyond the expiry of the biometrics. So, if the biometrics are set to expire in 2029, the Super Visa may only be valid until that date—even if the passport is valid until 2033 for example. If you want the Visa to be valid for a longer period, you can voluntarily provide new biometrics when applying, even if the previous ones haven't expired. Client who wish to voluntary re-enroll are required to pay the biometrics enrolment fee of $85.
